sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Part Two closed on a hand. Jesus said of His sheep, no one will snatch them out of my hand, and the next road ran to Bethany. Now John walks that Shepherd up to a sealed tomb. Underneath this whole chapter sits one question: does His hand still hold when the thing in the grave is someone you love — or you?

The dust has an answer for every promise Christ makes, and the answer is a hole in the ground. It says the grave is the one place His word does not reach. You can believe He forgives sin. You can believe He hears prayer. But you have stood at a graveside with your hat in your hands and watched the dirt go in, and the dust told you then what it tells you now: this is the end of the line, and faith is what men say to get through the afternoon.

It has a second lie, quieter than the first. When you pray for a sick man and nothing happens for two days, it tells you Jesus does not care. Love would have come running. So you learn to pray for the sick with one eye on the clock, and every hour He waits becomes evidence against Him. Some men stop praying for the dying at all. It hurts less to expect nothing.

Dust is where every man ends up, and the psalmist did not wait for his funeral to get there. He was already down in it when he prayed, My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) He did not ask God to make the dust comfortable. He asked to be made alive by a word. John 11 is that word, spoken by a Man who came four days after the burial and said, I am the resurrection and the life.

sections.heading: A Sickroom Near Jerusalem
pulls: The dust says the grave is the one place Christ’s word cannot reach. Jesus walked to a tomb four days shut and said, I am the resurrection and the life — not a day on the calendar, but a Man in the road.
paras: Jesus is across the Jordan when the message comes. He went there because the leaders in Jerusalem had picked up stones to kill Him, and the disciples have not forgotten it. Bethany, John tells you, was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away. To go to Lazarus is to walk back within reach of the men who want Him dead. John lets you feel that distance from the first verse.

This is the last sign John records before Jesus enters the city to die, and it is the sign that sets the plot against Him moving. Read John 11:1–27 in one sitting before you go further. Watch where the word love falls. Watch who misunderstands what. And mark the moment when a grieving woman, with her brother still in the grave, says what John wrote his whole book to bring you to say.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: LOVE BEFORE THE WAITING
paras: The sisters do not send a request. They send a name and a love. Lord, behold, he for whom you have great affection is sick. They do not tell Jesus what to do. They trust the love to tell Him. That is a good way to pray for a sick man.

Jesus answers before He moves. This sickness is not to death, but for the glory of God, that God’s Son may be glorified by it. He does not mean Lazarus will not die. Lazarus will die. He means death will not have the last word over this sickness. The last word will be God’s glory, shown in His Son.

Then John sets two sentences side by side, and the order is everything. Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. When therefore he heard that he was sick, he stayed two days in the place where he was. Loved, therefore stayed. John does not hand you the delay first and leave you to guess about the love. He writes the love down first, in plain words, so you cannot read the waiting without it. John does not tell you every reason for those two days, and you should not invent one. He tells you enough. The delay came out of the love, not out of its absence. When your own prayer sits a second day with no answer, the dust will read it as distance. Read it the way John wrote it. Jesus loved, and therefore He waited, and before the chapter ends you will see that the waiting was not wasted.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: GOING TO WAKE HIM
paras: Let’s go into Judea again. The disciples hear the word Judea and think of stones. Rabbi, the Jews were just trying to stone you. Are you going there again? Jesus answers with daylight. If a man walks in the day, he doesn’t stumble, because he sees the light of this world. His day has its twelve hours, set by His Father, and no stone in Jerusalem can cut it short by one. He walks toward danger because He walks in His Father’s time.

Then He tells them why He is going. Our friend, Lazarus, has fallen asleep, but I am going so that I may awake him out of sleep. Our friend. Jesus names Lazarus as His own and theirs. The disciples take Him at the surface. Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover. Sleep in a sick man is good news. So Jesus takes the soft word away. Lazarus is dead.

Mark that He used the soft word first, and meant it. For Jesus, death is sleep — not because death is small, but because He is the One who wakes. He also says the hard word plainly, because He does not lie to His men about the grave. Both are true at once. Lazarus is dead, and Jesus is going to wake him.

I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, so that you may believe. He is not glad Lazarus died. He is glad His men will see what He is about to do, because faith is what He came to give them. Thomas speaks up: Let’s go also, that we may die with him. He expects to be buried in Judea. He goes anyway. He does not yet see that the Man he follows is walking toward a grave to empty it.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: FOUR DAYS IN THE TOMB
pulls: Martha had the right day and the wrong distance. She had put the resurrection far down the road, at the last day — and the Resurrection was standing in front of her, asking whether she believed Him.
paras: He found that he had been in the tomb four days already. John counts the days so you will not soften them. Lazarus is not in a stupor. He is not mostly dead. He has been wrapped and laid behind a stone, and the house is full of people who came to console them concerning their brother. A real man, really dead, with a real tomb and a real crowd of mourners. That is the ground the sign is built on.

When Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary stayed in the house. Martha goes out on the road with her grief still raw, and the first thing out of her is the sentence every mourner has said to God in one form or another. Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died. It is honest. It is close to a charge. Then she adds what she still holds: Even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.

Jesus does not scold her. Your brother will rise again. Martha answers out of everything she has been taught. I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day. She is right. Jesus Himself had said, I will raise him up at the last day. There will be one great day when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and Martha believes it. Her faith is not wrong. It is incomplete. She has the right day and the wrong distance. She has put the resurrection far down the road, and the Resurrection is standing in front of her.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE RESURRECTION AND THE LIFE
paras: Now the sentence this volume is named for. I am the resurrection and the life. Jesus does not correct Martha’s calendar. He moves her hope from a date to a Person. The last day is still coming. But the power that will open the graves on it was standing on the road outside Bethany, dusty from the walk, talking with a woman who had just buried her brother.

Then He opens it in two halves. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. That is the believer whose body goes into the ground. He dies; the funeral is real; the dirt is real. And he lives. His body waits for the last day, when it will be raised, but he himself is not lost for one hour. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. That is the believer still walking around. Eternal life is not a wage he collects later. He holds it now, and the grave cannot take it back.

Then the question. Do you believe this? He does not ask how she feels. He asks whether she believes Him. The love, the waiting, the four days, the stone — all of it has come down to one woman on one road, asked one thing.

Her answer is the confession John wrote his book to draw out of you. Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son, he who comes into the world. Her brother is still in the tomb when she says it. She believes before she sees. John wrote that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name. Martha said yes. The same question is put to you, with your own grave somewhere ahead.

stations.verse: He said these things, and after that, he said to them, “Our friend, Lazarus, has fallen asleep, but I am going so that I may awake him out of sleep.
stations.question: Jesus called the dead Lazarus our friend and said, I am going so that I may awake him out of sleep; how does it change the way I face my own death to hear Him call it a sleep He will end?
stations.gloss: to wake out of sleep; to rouse
body: Exypnizō means to wake someone out of sleep. No other verse of the New Testament has it. The Greek Old Testament uses it when Samson awoke out of his sleep, and in Job’s bleak line about the dead: they will not awake, nor be roused out of their sleep.

Job looked into the grave and saw a sleep no one wakes from. Jesus looks into the same grave and says He is going to Bethany to do the waking. For the One who speaks here, death is a sleep, because He is the One who rouses the sleeper.

The dust says the grave is a door that opens only one way. Jesus calls Lazarus our friend and sets out to wake him. If you belong to Christ, that is how He speaks of your grave too. Your death will be real, and it will not be final. He will come to it the way a father comes to wake his boy before first light.
stations.live: Think of a believer you have buried — a father, a grandmother, an old friend. Say his name aloud this week with Christ’s words over it: ‘He has fallen asleep, and Jesus is going to wake him.’

stations.verse: Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he spoke of taking rest in sleep.
stations.question: The disciples thought Jesus meant taking rest in sleep, so He told them plainly, Lazarus is dead; what hard thing in my life do I keep calling by a softer name instead of letting Jesus name it?
stations.gloss: a lying down; a resting in sleep
body: Koimēsis names a lying down, a resting. It occurs in this one verse of the New Testament, in John’s note on what the disciples thought Jesus meant. They heard the plain sense, and in a sick man that is good news. Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.

John tells you they had it wrong, and Jesus did not leave them there. He said it straight. A man reaches for the soft word for his own reasons. The marriage is going through a quiet stretch. The second drink is just how you unwind. Your prayer life is resting. Soft names keep the dead thing in its room, where no one has to go in.

The dust likes soft names because soft names need no Savior. Jesus names death plainly, and in the next breath He says, Nevertheless, let’s go to him. He does not name a death to walk away from it. He names it because He is going there.
stations.live: Name one thing in your life that is dead and has been wearing a softer name. Say the plain word to God this week, then pray the next sentence too: ‘Lord, this is dead. Come to it.’

stations.verse: Many of the Jews had joined the women around Martha and Mary, to console them concerning their brother.
stations.question: Many came to Bethany to console them concerning their brother, and their comfort was real but could not open a grave; when grief comes into my house, what comfort do I lean on before I bring it to Christ?
stations.gloss: to comfort, console; to encourage
body: Paramytheomai means to encourage or exhort, and to comfort or console. It turns up in four verses of the New Testament. Two are in this chapter, of the crowd in the sisters’ house. The other two are Paul’s, writing to the church at Thessalonica, where he tells them to encourage the faint-hearted.

John does not fault the neighbors. They came, they sat, they grieved with the sisters, and that is a good thing for men to do. But consolation sits beside the grave. It cannot open one. The best of them went home that night with Lazarus still behind the stone. A hand on the shoulder is a kindness. It is not a resurrection.

The dust says comfort is the most you can hope for at a graveside — kind words, a covered dish, a long drive home. Christ comes to Bethany carrying more than consolation. He comes as the One who will undo the reason for it.
stations.live: When grief rises this week, bring it to Christ first, in two plain sentences, before you reach for the remote or the bottle. Then take the comfort men offer as a gift from Him, not a stand-in for Him.

stations.verse: Then when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary stayed in the house.
stations.question: When Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went out and met Him on the road with her grief still raw; what loss have I not yet carried out to Him because I am waiting until I can speak of it calmly?
stations.gloss: to go to meet; to meet on the way
body: Hypantaō means to go to meet someone, to meet him on the way. Ten verses of the New Testament use it. John uses it of the official’s servants who met him on the road with the news Your child lives. Matthew uses it of the morning the tomb stood open, when Jesus met them.

Martha did not wait in the house until her face was right. She went out and met Him with the hardest sentence she had: Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died. Jesus did not send her back to tidy it. He answered her with the greatest word in the chapter.

The dust says stay inside until you can come to Him calm. But He was already coming. And when His own tomb stood empty, the risen Christ met His people on the road. You go out to meet a Savior who is already on His way to you.
stations.live: Pray your hardest sentence to Christ this week exactly as it is, unpolished, the way Martha did. Then read John 11:23–26 slowly and let His answer to her stand as His answer to you.

stations.verse: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies.
stations.question: Martha believed her brother would rise at the last day, and Jesus answered, I am the resurrection and the life; how does trusting a living Person, and not only a future date, change the way I stand at a grave this week?
stations.gloss: a rising up; resurrection from the dead
body: Anastasis means a raising up, a rising, and above all a rising from the dead. It stands in forty verses of the New Testament. It names Christ’s own rising and the general resurrection. John uses it of that last day, when some come out to the resurrection of life and others to the resurrection of judgment.

Martha used the word for an event. Jesus used it for Himself, as the One who brings it about. The event is still coming — one resurrection of the just and the unjust when Christ returns. But the power behind that day already had a name, and Martha was talking to Him.

The dust says resurrection is a doctrine you will think about at the end. Peter says God caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. The hope is living because the Resurrection is alive, and He has already begun His work in you.
stations.live: Write John 11:25–26 on a card and keep it in your shirt pocket all week. Each time your hand finds it, answer His question out loud: ‘Yes, Lord. I believe You.’

practices.title: READ THE LOVE FIRST
practices.body: John set Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus ahead of the two days of waiting, so you would never read the waiting without the love. Write down the prayer that has gone longest without an answer — the sick father, the son who left, the work that will not come. Above it, write John 11:5. Each time you pray it this week, say the love first and the request second. Let the order of the verse set the order of your praying.

practices.title: SAY THE PLAIN WORD
practices.body: Jesus told His men plainly, Lazarus is dead. Do the same in your own house. Sit down with your wife this week — or a brother, if you live alone — and talk plainly about your own death: where the papers are, who gets called, and which Scripture you want read at the grave. Choose John 11:25–26, and tell her why. A man who can speak of his grave with the Resurrection in view is not being grim. He is free.

practices.title: GO TO A HOUSE OF GRIEF
practices.body: Many came to Bethany to console them concerning their brother, and John does not fault them for it. Think of one man who has buried someone this year. Go see him, or call and set a time. Do not bring a speech. Sit, ask about the one he lost, and listen. Before you leave, tell him one thing Jesus said at a graveside. You cannot open the tomb. You can point him to the One who stood outside it and spoke.

practices.title: READ IT AT THE TABLE
practices.body: John wrote this account so that ordinary people would believe. Read John 11:1–27 aloud at supper one night this week, to whoever sits at your table. Then ask two things: what did Martha believe before Jesus came, and what did He tell her? Let the youngest answer first. You do not need to preach. Let the text do the work it was written to do, and let your house hear the question Jesus asked.

practices.title: ANSWER WITH MARTHA
practices.body: Jesus asked, Do you believe this? and waited for an answer. Each morning this week, before you check the phone, read John 11:25–27 aloud and answer with Martha’s words: Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son. Then read John 20:31, the reason John wrote it all down. Say it on the good days, so the words are already in your mouth on the bad one.

title: He Who Believes Will Live
subtitle: from dust to the life that death cannot keep
keyVerse: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies.

passage.text: Now a certain man was sick, Lazarus from Bethany, of the village of Mary and her sister, Martha.
It was that Mary who had anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother, Lazarus, was sick.
The sisters therefore sent to him, saying, “Lord, behold, he for whom you have great affection is sick.”
But when Jesus heard it, he said, “This sickness is not to death, but for the glory of God, that God’s Son may be glorified by it.”
Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus.
When therefore he heard that he was sick, he stayed two days in the place where he was.
Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let’s go into Judea again.”
The disciples asked him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just trying to stone you. Are you going there again?”
Jesus answered, “Aren’t there twelve hours of daylight? If a man walks in the day, he doesn’t stumble, because he sees the light of this world.
But if a man walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light isn’t in him.”
He said these things, and after that, he said to them, “Our friend, Lazarus, has fallen asleep, but I am going so that I may awake him out of sleep.”
The disciples therefore said, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”
Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he spoke of taking rest in sleep.
So Jesus said to them plainly then, “Lazarus is dead.
I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, so that you may believe. Nevertheless, let’s go to him.”
Thomas therefore, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples, “Let’s go also, that we may die with him.”
So when Jesus came, he found that he had been in the tomb four days already.
Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away.
Many of the Jews had joined the women around Martha and Mary, to console them concerning their brother.
Then when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary stayed in the house.
Therefore Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.
Even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”
Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.”
Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.”
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies.
Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”
She said to him, “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son, he who comes into the world.”

stationsIntro: Read each verse slowly, out loud if the house is still quiet, the way you would read word from a friend who is already on his way. Answer plainly, and let the Greek word bring you back to the One who went to Bethany to wake His friend.
lifeIntro: Christ went back into Judea for a dead friend, and He said over the grave what no other man can say. He is the resurrection and the life, and He asks you whether you believe it. Answer Him this week in five plain ways. None of them earns a thing; each one leans on what He has said.
lifePulls: Love came first, and the waiting came out of it. Lazarus was four days in the grave, and the One who is the resurrection and the life was already on the road.
prayer: Father, You sent Your Son to Bethany, and He walked back into danger for a friend. Thank You that Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus, and that His love came before the waiting. Thank You that He is the resurrection and the life, and that I can trust Him with every grave. When my prayers wait, teach me to read the waiting by the love. Forgive me for the soft names I give to dead things, and for keeping my grief indoors instead of bringing it to Him. Comfort the ones I know who are burying someone this year, and let me point them to Christ. When my own day comes, keep me believing that I will live, even though I die. Yes, Lord. I believe that Jesus is the Christ, Your Son, who came into the world. In Jesus’ name, amen.
