bottomLine: Jesus loved Lazarus and his sisters, and because He loved them He waited two days. He walked back toward men with stones to wake a friend He called asleep, and He came to a tomb where Lazarus had lain four days. Martha believed in a resurrection at the last day. Jesus told her He is the resurrection and the life. Believe Him. The man who believes in Christ will live even if he dies, and death cannot keep him.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and watch who is coming up the Bethany road. Lift them to the One who heard that His friend was sick and loved the whole house. Lift them to the One who walked back toward the stones because a friend lay in a grave. Lift them to the One who stood outside a tomb four days shut and was not too late, because the Resurrection is never too late to a death.

The dust has kept you company at every graveside you have stood beside. It told you the hole in the ground was the end of the line, that faith was a thing men say to get through the service, and that two days of silence meant God did not care. You have believed some of it. You may have believed it about your own grave most of all — that when they lower you down, Christ’s hand lets go there.

Hear what He said on the road. I am the resurrection and the life. Not a day on a far calendar, but a Man with dust on His feet. He did not promise Martha that grief would be skipped. Her brother was dead, and Jesus did not pretend otherwise. He promised that the one who believes in Him will still live, even if he dies, and He backed the promise with His own body. At the Passover John says was near, He would go into a tomb Himself, and He would walk out of it alive, the first of the harvest.

So carry this into Tuesday, and into the day they carry you. If you believe in Him, you will die, and you will live. Your body will be laid down like seed and raised imperishable at the last day, when every grave hears His voice. And the life He has given you now — the life you hold this morning — will never die between here and there. He asked Martha, and He asks you: Do you believe this? Say yes. Lazarus was His friend, and Jesus said, I am going so that I may awake him out of sleep. He says the same over every man who believes in Him, and He will say it over you.
closingVerse: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies.
carry: Jesus told Martha that the one who believes in Him will still live, even if he dies, and then asked, Do you believe this? — which grave, your own or another’s, do you most need to carry under that promise this week?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Some things smell like the end. A barn after the flood water goes down. A freezer left shut through a week without power. You open the door and step back, and nobody has to tell you there is nothing left to save. You carry a few rooms like that. The sin that has gone on so long it has a smell. The marriage that went quiet years ago. The brother you have not spoken to since the funeral. You keep those doors shut, because you already know what is behind them.

The dust has a name for those places. Too far gone. It says Christ can help a man who is struggling, but not a man who is dead. It says He can mend what is cracked, but not what has rotted. And it slips a second lie under the first: if He ever did come near, He would come with a clean, dry eye, like an inspector with a clipboard, untouched by what He found.

You do not need anyone to tell you that you are made of dust. You can smell it on yourself. So say it the way it was said by a man lying flat in it: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) That is a prayer for the far gone, and it asks for nothing small. It asks for life, and it asks for it by a word.

John 11 gives you that word, cried out in a loud voice at the mouth of a four-day tomb: Lazarus, come out. Before Jesus says it, He weeps. After He says it, the men who saw it start planning His death. All three belong to this week, and all three are for you.

sections.heading: From a Graveside to a Council Room
pulls: The dust says some things are too far gone — four days gone, past the smell. Jesus wept at the grave, asked for the stone to be moved anyway, and called a dead man by name. The far gone are exactly the ones He raises.
paras: This week picks up on the road outside Bethany, where Martha has just confessed that Jesus is the Christ, God’s Son. Her brother is still in the tomb. Now she goes back for her sister, and the chapter moves from the road to the grave, and from the grave to a room in Jerusalem where the rulers of the nation sit down to decide what to do about a Man who raises the dead.

Read John 11:28–57 straight through. Watch how much of it turns on seeing. Jesus sees the weeping. The mourners say come and see. Many see and believe; others see and go to report. And watch the turn at the end. The sign that gave Lazarus back his life is the sign that settles Jesus’ death. The high priest says more than he knows, and John tells you what God meant by it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: HE GROANED, AND HE WEPT
paras: Martha finds her sister and speaks low. The Teacher is here and is calling you. Mary rises quickly and goes, and the mourners follow, sure that She is going to the tomb to weep there. She goes to Jesus instead. She falls at His feet and says the sentence her sister said on the road: Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.

Then John shows you what death does to the Son of God. When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled. The word for groaned is hard, and it carries anger. Jesus stands among the mourners and is moved, deep in His spirit, against what He sees. John does not open every room of His heart, and you should not pretend to. He tells you enough. The Son of God was not calm in the face of death.

Where have you laid him? They answer, Lord, come and see. Then John writes the shortest verse in his book. Jesus wept. The Word who was with God in the beginning stands at a friend’s grave with tears on His face. He is true God, and He is truly a man, and His tears are real tears.

The crowd splits over them. Some say, See how much affection he had for him. Others ask, Couldn’t this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying? Jesus does not weep because He has run out of power. In a few minutes He will empty the tomb. He weeps anyway. The One about to raise the dead does not skip the grief of the people He loves. He walks into it with them.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: TAKE AWAY THE STONE
paras: Jesus therefore, again groaning in himself, came to the tomb. Now it was a cave, and a stone lay against it. The anger has not cooled on the walk. He comes to the grave the way a man comes to the thing that has hurt his family. And His first word there is an order to the living. Take away the stone. Men will do the lifting. Only He will do the raising.

Martha objects, and she is not wrong about the facts. Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days. She knows what four days do to a body. Nobody in Bethany thinks there is anything behind that stone but rot. That is exactly the ground Jesus chose. He does not raise men who are mostly alive.

Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory? He points her back to His word. Faith here is not pretending the stench is not there. It is trusting what He said more than what the air is telling her. So they took away the stone from the place where the dead man was lying. The smell came out first. The glory came after.

Then Jesus prays aloud, with His eyes lifted. Father, I thank you that you listened to me. He gives thanks before the grave opens. And He says why He prays where the crowd can hear: that they may believe that you sent me. The sign is the Father bearing witness to the Son, so that people standing at the edge of a grave will believe.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: LAZARUS, COME OUT
pulls: Lazarus did not decide to live. He could not hear, could not move, could not want anything. Then the Son of God called him by name, and the dead man came out. That is how every man comes to life.
paras: When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice. Jesus does not whisper. He does not plead with the dead or coax them. He commands. Lazarus, come out. Three words, and the one who obeys them is a dead man. Lazarus did not decide to live. He could not hear, could not move, could not want anything. The voice that called him gave him the ears to hear it.

He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. John still calls him He who was dead as he comes through the doorway of the cave. He comes out dressed for burial. Every bit of the life is Christ’s doing. Lazarus brought nothing to it but a corpse.

That is how any man comes to God. You were not sick when Christ found you. Paul says God made us alive together with Christ — even when we were dead through our trespasses. The new birth is not a dead man’s good decision. It is the Son calling a man by name, and the man coming out. Jesus had already told you where this is headed: the hour comes in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice. Lazarus came out early, and he would die again. On the last day the same voice will empty every grave, and those He raises to life will never go back in.

Free him, and let him go. The life was Christ’s alone. The unwrapping He handed to the people standing there. Men who had come to weep now put their hands on the grave bands of a living man. It still goes that way. Christ raises; His people loosen.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: ONE MAN FOR THE PEOPLE
paras: Many of the Jews who came to Mary and saw what Jesus did believed in him. That is what the sign was for. But some of them went away to the Pharisees. The same tomb, the same voice, the same living man — and some believed while others went to report. A sign does not change a heart by itself. A man can stand close enough to smell the grave and still walk away from the One who emptied it. Only grace opens blind eyes.

The council meets. What are we doing? For this man does many signs. They do not deny the signs. They fear them. If we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation. A dead man walking out of his tomb is, to them, a problem to be managed.

Then Caiaphas, being high priest that year, speaks with contempt. You know nothing at all. And he gives them the cold arithmetic: it is advantageous for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish. Spend one man, keep the rest.

John stops you there. Now he didn’t say this of himself. Caiaphas meant a killing. God meant the gospel. He prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, John says, and not for the nation only, but that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad. One Man dying in the place of the people, so the people do not perish. That is substitution, and it reaches past Israel to scattered children of God in every nation — men like you. So from that day forward they took counsel that they might put him to death. The life Jesus gave Lazarus would cost Him His own.

stations.verse: When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled.
stations.question: When Jesus saw Mary and her friends weeping, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled, minutes before He undid that death; what changes in my own grieving when I see that Christ was not calm about death?
stations.gloss: to be moved with anger; to be deeply stirred
body: Embrimaomai was used of horses snorting, and from there of speaking or acting with deep feeling. In the New Testament it means to be moved with anger, or to warn someone sternly. Five verses hold it. Mark uses it when Jesus strictly warned a leper He had just healed. John uses it twice in this chapter.

Set that weight beside the grave in Bethany. Jesus did not stand there with the calm of a man who does not care. Something in Him rose against what He saw. John does not lay out every reason, and you should not fill in what he left out. He tells you this much: Christ was not neutral about death.

The dust says God looks at your losses with a shrug. Christ walked to Lazarus’ tomb stirred to anger. Paul calls death The last enemy that will be abolished, and the One who was angry at it is the One who will finish it.
stations.live: When anger or grief rises in you over a death this week, do not bury it as unspiritual. Bring it to the Christ who groaned at Lazarus’ grave: ‘You hate this more than I do, and You came to end it.’

stations.verse: Jesus wept.
stations.question: Jesus wept at Lazarus’ grave, though He knew He would raise him within the hour; what grief have I kept from Christ because I thought a man with real faith should stay dry-eyed?
stations.gloss: to weep; to shed tears
body: Dakryō means to weep, to shed tears. This verse is its only place in the New Testament. When John tells of Mary and the mourners weeping two verses earlier, he uses a different word, klaiō. For Jesus he uses this one. Their weeping and His tears stand side by side at the same grave.

Two words, and they carry the whole Christ. The Word who was with God stood at a grave with wet eyes. He knew what He was about to do, and He wept anyway. Grief and sure hope stood in the same Man at the same tomb, and neither one cancelled the other.

The dust says your tears mean your faith has failed, or else that God has none for you. Christ answers both. Your faith does not need to be dry. And your High Priest is not one who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities. He has stood where you stand.
stations.live: Name one loss you have never wept over in front of God — a parent, a child, a friendship, a marriage. Sit with it before Him this week, and let what comes, come. He wept first.

stations.verse: Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of him who was dead, said to him, “Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.
stations.question: Jesus said, Take away the stone, and Martha answered, by this time there is a stench; where have I let the plain facts of a dead thing outweigh what Christ has said He will do?
stations.gloss: to give off a smell; to stink
body: Ozō means to give off a smell. Martha’s warning is the only verse in the New Testament that uses it. The Greek Old Testament uses it once, when the frogs of Egypt died and were heaped up and the land stank. It is the plain word for what death leaves behind.

Martha is not faithless. She is honest. Four days is four days, and everyone in Bethany knows what is behind the stone. That is the very ground Jesus chose for this sign. He raised a man past every human hope, so that no one could say the man had only been sleeping, or only weak, or only mostly gone.

The dust says leave the stone where it is; some things are better kept shut. Christ asks for the stone because He means to speak into what lies behind it. Your rot does not turn Him back. He came to call the dead out of it.
stations.live: Name the place you have sealed off as too far gone — an old sin, a cold marriage, a brother you wrote off. Pray about it aloud this week with the stone off: ‘Lord, it stinks. Speak into it anyway.’

stations.verse: He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Free him, and let him go.
stations.question: Lazarus came out alive by Christ’s word alone, and then Jesus told the people standing there, Free him, and let him go; which man near me, newly raised by Christ, is still bound in ways my hands could help loosen?
stations.gloss: grave bands; strips wound around a body
body: Keiria is a plain, everyday word. Here it means the bands wound around a body for burial. The Greek Old Testament uses it once, in Proverbs 7:16, for what is spread over a couch. In the New Testament it appears only here, wrapped around a living man.

Lazarus walked out still dressed for the grave — bound hand and foot, his face wrapped. The life was Christ’s work alone. The unwrapping took hands, and Jesus gave that work to the people standing around. Free him, and let him go.

The dust says a man who has been raised ought to come out clean, and that the church’s job is to inspect him. Christ says loosen him. New believers come out with the smell of the tomb still on them. Your hands are part of how Christ frees them.
stations.live: Find a man newer to the faith than you. This week, do one practical thing for him — a ride to church, an hour in the Gospel of John together, a hard conversation he cannot face alone.

stations.verse: Nor do you consider that it is advantageous for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish.
stations.question: Caiaphas meant a political killing, but God meant the cross when the high priest said one man should die for the people; what guilt am I still trying to pay off myself instead of resting it on that Man?
stations.gloss: to be of advantage; to be profitable
body: Sympherō can mean to bring together, but in the New Testament it mostly stands on its own: it is profitable, it is to your advantage. Fifteen verses carry it. Caiaphas uses it here, and John points back to his words when Jesus is led away bound. Jesus uses it Himself in the upper room: It is to your advantage that I go away.

Caiaphas did a ledger sum. One man’s life on one side, a nation’s safety on the other. He was right, and he had no idea why. God took a schemer’s sentence and made it preach the cross: one Man dying in the place of many, so the many do not perish.

The dust says your guilt is yours to pay down, a little each month. The advantage Caiaphas could not see is yours. One Man died for the people. The debt was laid on Him, and the man who believes in Him will not perish.
stations.live: Write down the guilt you keep making payments on. Across it write John 11:50: one man should die for the people. Then stop paying, and thank Him for the payment already made.

practices.title: GRIEVE IN FRONT OF HIM
practices.body: Jesus wept, and He has not changed. Set aside half an hour this week, alone, with John 11:28–37 open. Read it slowly. Then name to God, out loud, the loss you have carried dry-eyed — the father you buried, the child you lost, the friend who turned on you. Do not hurry it or try to fix it. Let the One who groaned at Lazarus’ grave sit with you at yours. Grief brought to Christ is not a lapse of faith.

practices.title: MOVE ONE STONE
practices.body: Martha said there would be a stench, and Jesus said, Take away the stone. Pick the one place you have kept sealed — the sin you have never told anyone, the money nobody sees, the old hurt with your wife. Tell one trusted brother about it this week, plainly. You are not opening the grave to show off the rot. You are opening it because Christ speaks to what lies behind stones, and you want to hear Him.

practices.title: PRAY BY NAME
practices.body: Jesus did not call out to the dead in general. He called Lazarus. Write down the names of three men you know who are dead toward God. Pray for each by name every day this week. Ask the Father to do for them what He did for you: to speak, through His Son, into a grave no man can open. Then watch for one open door to tell one of them what Christ has done.

practices.title: NAME YOUR PLACE
practices.body: The council saw a dead man walk out of his tomb and worried about our place and our nation. A man can do the same — guard his standing, his money, his way of running the house, and keep Jesus at arm’s length to protect it. Ask God this week to show you one place you are guarding against Christ’s claim on you. Then hand it over to the One who died to gather His people, not to take from them.

practices.title: REST ON THE ONE MAN
practices.body: Caiaphas said more than he knew: one man would die for the people. Each morning this week, read Isaiah 53:4–6 and John 11:49–52 side by side. Then say aloud, with your own name in it, what John says the high priest prophesied: Jesus died in my place, so I will not perish. When the old guilt comes at midday, answer it with that sentence. Nothing else needs adding to it.

title: Lazarus, Come Out
subtitle: from dust to a tomb left empty
keyVerse: When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!

passage.text: When she had said this, she went away and called Mary, her sister, secretly, saying, “The Teacher is here and is calling you.”
When she heard this, she arose quickly and went to him.
Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was in the place where Martha met him.
Then the Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary, that she rose up quickly and went out, followed her, saying, “She is going to the tomb to weep there.”
Therefore when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.”
When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled,
and said, “Where have you laid him?” They told him, “Lord, come and see.”
Jesus wept.
The Jews therefore said, “See how much affection he had for him!”
Some of them said, “Couldn’t this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying?”
Jesus therefore, again groaning in himself, came to the tomb. Now it was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of him who was dead, said to him, “Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.”
Jesus said to her, “Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory?”
So they took away the stone from the place where the dead man was lying. Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, “Father, I thank you that you listened to me.
I know that you always listen to me, but because of the multitude standing around I said this, that they may believe that you sent me.”
When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!”
He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Free him, and let him go.”
Therefore many of the Jews who came to Mary and saw what Jesus did believed in him.
But some of them went away to the Pharisees and told them the things which Jesus had done.
The chief priests therefore and the Pharisees gathered a council, and said, “What are we doing? For this man does many signs.
If we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”
But a certain one of them, Caiaphas, being high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all,
nor do you consider that it is advantageous for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish.”
Now he didn’t say this of himself, but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation,
and not for the nation only, but that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.
So from that day forward they took counsel that they might put him to death.
Jesus therefore walked no more openly among the Jews, but departed from there into the country near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim. He stayed there with his disciples.
Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand. Many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover, to purify themselves.
Then they sought for Jesus and spoke with one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think—that he isn’t coming to the feast at all?”
Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had commanded that if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, that they might seize him.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE OPEN TOMB
stationsIntro: Take these verses one at a time, the way you would walk a back field after a storm to see what is still standing. Answer each question in plain words, and let the Greek word walk you back to the tomb Jesus emptied.
lifeIntro: The Son of God stood at a friend’s grave, wept, and called a dead man out by name. Then He set His face toward the death that would pay for it all. Answer Him this week in five ways — not to raise yourself, which no man can do, but as a man who has heard the voice.
lifePulls: Jesus wept at a grave He was about to empty, asked for a stone the whole town wanted left alone, and called a dead man by name. Then He went to die so the dead could live.
prayer: Father, Your Son stood at Lazarus’ grave and wept. Thank You that He was not calm about death, and that He came to destroy it. Thank You that He called a dead man by name, and that He called me when I was dead. I bring You the grief I have carried dry-eyed, and the places I have sealed off as too far gone. Speak into them the way Jesus spoke at the tomb. Give me hands to help unwrap the men You are raising around me. Thank You that one Man died for the people, so that I will not perish. Keep me listening for His voice until the day every grave hears it. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, Your Son stood at Lazarus’ grave and wept.
Thank You that He was not calm about death, and that He came to destroy it.
Thank You that He called a dead man by name, and that He called me when I
was dead.
I bring You the grief I have carried dry-eyed, and the places I have sealed off as
too far gone.
Speak into them the way Jesus spoke at the tomb.
Give me hands to help unwrap the men You are raising around me.
Thank You that one Man died for the people, so that I will not perish.
Keep me listening for His voice until the day every grave hears it.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: At Lazarus’ grave Jesus groaned in anger at death and wept real tears, though He knew what He was about to do. Martha warned of the stench; He had the stone moved anyway and called a man four days dead out by name. Then the council planned His death, and the high priest preached the gospel without knowing it: one Man dying for the people. Nothing in you is too far gone for that voice.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul. A Man is standing at the mouth of the cave. See the tears still on His face. See the anger at death still in His chest. See Him order the stone moved that everyone wanted left alone. And hear Him — not whispering, not pleading, but crying out in a loud voice the name of a man four days dead.

The dust has told you that some things are past saving, and you have believed it about the shut rooms in your own life. It has told you God looks on your grief with a dry eye. It has told you that if Christ ever came near your grave, He would hold His nose and keep His distance. Every one of those lies died at Bethany. He came near. He wept. He asked for the stone. The stench did not turn Him back.

And then He went and paid for it. Caiaphas said one man should die for the people, and God made those words true in a way the high priest never meant. Jesus walked out of Bethany toward the cross. He gave His life in the place of yours, so that the scattered children of God would be gathered into one, and you among them. And the Man who raised Lazarus did not stay in His own grave. When Peter went into that tomb, the linen cloths were lying there, and the cloth that had been on His head was rolled up in a place by itself. No grave bands held Him.

So carry this into Tuesday. The voice that said Lazarus, come out is the voice that called you out of death into life, and it is the voice you will hear again. Jesus said the hour comes in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice. When your body is laid down, that hour is coming for you. He will call your name the way He called Lazarus. The grave bands will not hold you, and you will never go back in.
closingVerse: When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!
carry: Jesus cried, Lazarus, come out, and a man who could do nothing for himself walked out alive; where do you most need to remember this week that your life with God began with His voice, not your effort?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: You were raised to count. A man figures the board feet before he cuts, the fuel before the trip, the payment before he signs. That is no sin. It is how a roof stays on and a family stays fed. But the dust takes that good habit and walks it somewhere it was never meant to go. It follows you into the presence of Christ and starts adding.

The dust says love for God should be sensible. Give Him a slice of your Sunday, a share of what is left when the bills are paid, and call it wisdom. Anything past that is waste, and a practical man ought to be embarrassed by it. And when the dust is not telling you that you give too much, it turns around and tells you that you have not given enough — that God is waiting on your next payment before He moves, that every prayer is a down payment on His favor, and that the bad news in your house this year is the bill coming due.

Both lies get the order wrong. One makes Christ a cost to keep low. The other makes Him a seller to be paid. A man who believes them both ends up face down, too careful to love and too anxious to rest, with one honest prayer left in him: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)

John 12 answers with a supper. A man who lay four days in the grave sits at the table. His sister breaks open the costliest thing in the house and pours it on the feet of the One who called him out. She is not buying anything. She is answering what has already been given.

sections.heading: Six Days Before the Passover
pulls: Mary did not pour out the nard to get her brother back. He was already at the table, alive. That is the order of the gospel: Christ gives first, and love answers with whatever it has.
paras: Chapter 11 ended with a death sentence. From the day Lazarus walked out of the tomb, the council took counsel that they might put him to death, and Jesus walked no more openly among the Jews. He stayed with His disciples in a town called Ephraim, near the wilderness. Now the Passover is close, the crowds in the temple are asking whether He will come to the feast at all, and He comes — first to Bethany, to the house where the stone was rolled away.

John has already told you who this Mary is. Back in 11:2 he named her as the one who had anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, before he ever told you about the tomb. She is the sister who fell at Jesus’ feet and wept when He finally came. Read 12:1–11 straight through. Watch the table, watch Mary, watch Judas, and watch where Jesus turns every eye in the room: to His own burial.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: A SUPPER AT BETHANY
paras: Then six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, who had been dead, whom he raised from the dead. John will not let you forget who lives in this house. In one verse he ties Lazarus to the grave three times: where Lazarus was, who had been dead, whom He raised. The man at this supper did not have a close call. He had been buried. The smell of the tomb had been on him. Now he eats.

So they made him a supper there. The supper is for Jesus. It is a house giving thanks the way a house knows how — with food, a table, and the people who belong around it. Martha served, but Lazarus was one of those who sat at the table with him. Martha does what she always does, and John does not scold her for it. Lazarus does what a living man does. He sits and eats with the One who gave him back his breath.

Mark where all of this begins. Nothing in this house was earned. The family did not get their brother back because their love for Jesus was large enough. Jesus loved them first — John said it plainly, Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus — and then He came, and wept, and called. Grace walked up to the grave before anyone in this house had a thing to offer.

That is your story too, if you belong to Christ. You were the one in the grave. He called you out. Every honest thing you do for Him this week is a supper given in thanks, not a payment made in advance. Sit at His table first. The serving comes after.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A POUND OF PURE NARD
paras: Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair. Look at the first word. Therefore. What Mary does flows out of what Jesus has done. Her brother is across the room, alive. That is the reason, and John puts it in one word.

John gives you the measure: a full pound, pure, very precious. Judas will put a number on it in a moment. Mary does not measure it out by drops. She pours it on His feet, and then she wipes them with her hair. John does not explain the gesture, and you do not need him to. A woman bent to the floor before the One who had stood weeping at her brother’s tomb, and spent the most costly thing she had on Him.

The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment. A few days before, the word in this family’s mouth had been stench. Martha had warned Him at the tomb: by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days. Now the same family sits in a house filled with another smell. Death had been answered, and love filled the rooms.

That is what it looks like when grace lands on a person. Not a careful percentage. Not a hedge against next year. Mary is not trying to buy the favor of Jesus; she already has it, and her brother is the proof. She spends herself on Him because He is worth it and because He has already spent Himself on her. Love that answers grace does not keep the receipt.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE THIEF AT THE TABLE
pulls: Jesus set His own grave in the middle of the supper. Mary poured out what she had kept; He was about to pour out His life. Every gift you bring Him answers that.
paras: Then a voice cuts across the fragrance. Then Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, one of his disciples, who would betray him, said, Why wasn’t this ointment sold for three hundred denarii, and given to the poor? On its face, the question sounds responsible. Three hundred denarii is real money, and the poor are real people. A careful man nods along.

But John will not let the question stand in its good clothes. Now he said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the money box, used to steal what was put into it. John calls him what he was. A thief. Not a man with a spending problem. Not a disciple going through a hard season. One of the twelve, trusted with the common purse, had been taking from it, and he used the poor as cover for his complaint.

Set the two side by side. Mary and Judas sat at the same supper, near the same Jesus, after the same miracle. One poured. One grasped. John names Judas plainly, and so should you, because the warning here is not about money in general. It is about how near a man can sit to Christ and still be keeping his own box.

And Jesus knew. John has already set down His word that one of the twelve is a devil, and that he spoke of Judas. He knew what was in the box and whose hand was in it. Nothing hidden in your life is news to Him either. That knowledge frightens a man only until he sees what Jesus is about to do for sinners whose hands are not clean. He is going to die for them.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: KEPT FOR HIS BURIAL
paras: Jesus answers for Mary before she can answer for herself. Leave her alone. She has kept this for the day of my burial. He does not argue the price. He reads her gift by His own death. Six days from the Passover, with the council already plotting, Jesus sets His grave in the middle of the supper. Whatever else her ointment meant, He tells the room what it means now: it belongs to His burial.

For you always have the poor with you, but you don’t always have me. That is no shrug at the poor, and no leave to stop giving. Jesus is telling the room what time it is. The poor would still be at the gate next month. The Son of God would be in a tomb before the week was out.

Then the story swings outward. A large crowd therefore of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came, not for Jesus’ sake only, but that they might see Lazarus also. A living man is hard to argue with. So the chief priests make the only plan left to men who cannot answer him. The chief priests conspired to put Lazarus to death also, because on account of him many of the Jews went away and believed in Jesus.

Look at what they are trying to do. Kill the man Jesus raised, as if a grave could keep someone the Resurrection had already called out. They would bury Lazarus again to stop men from believing. Jesus is about to go into the grave Himself for the opposite reason — that men would believe, and believing, have life in His name. Because He goes into it, the grave has lost its claim on every man He calls.

stations.verse: Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.
stations.question: Mary poured her ointment on Jesus at a table where her brother, lately four days in the grave, sat alive; what has Christ already done for me that I have answered only with what costs me little?
stations.gloss: ointment; a fragrant oil for anointing
body: Myron is ointment. In the Greek Old Testament it often stands for the Hebrew word for oil, as in the precious oil on the head that ran down Aaron’s beard in Psalm 133. It appears in thirteen New Testament verses, and in all but one of them the ointment is for Jesus.

Luke closes his account of the cross with the women who prepared spices and ointments for His body. Mary of Bethany poured hers out while He still sat at the table, while He could watch her do it. She answered the life He had just given her brother, and He received it.

The dust says Christ gets what is left once the sensible things are paid for. The most costly thing in the house went on His feet, and He called it good. Your love cannot buy Him. It can only answer Him, and He does not despise the answer.
stations.live: Name one thing you have held back from Christ because it costs too much — an hour, a sum, a hard conversation. Give it this week, not to earn anything. Say: ‘He gave first. This is my answer.’

stations.verse: Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.
stations.question: Mary spent a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious on Jesus’ feet and bent to wipe them with her hair; where does my worship of Christ stay careful because I do not want to look foolish?
stations.gloss: nard; a fragrant ointment made from a plant of that name
body: Nardos names an Indian plant and the fragrant ointment made from it. It stands in only two New Testament verses, both at Bethany. Mark calls it ointment of pure nard—very costly; John calls it pure nard, very precious. In the Greek Old Testament it turns up in the Song of Solomon: my perfume spread its fragrance.

Two gospel writers stop to tell you what it was worth, and neither is impressed by it for its own sake. What matters is where the nard went. Not on a project or a cause. On Jesus, at His feet, all of it, while a disciple sat nearby doing the math.

The dust wants you to hold your most precious thing in reserve, in case Christ turns out not to be enough. But the nard was safest spent. Whatever you pour on Him is kept where nothing can reach it — with the Son who was about to be buried and would not stay buried.
stations.live: Write down the one thing you would hate most to lose. Hold it up to Christ by name in prayer this week, and tell Him plainly: ‘You are worth more than this. It is Yours.’

stations.verse: Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.
stations.question: Days after Martha warned of a stench at the tomb, the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment; what has Christ brought from death to life in my own house that I have never thanked Him for aloud?
stations.gloss: a smell; an odor that fills a place
body: Osmē is a smell, an odor. It comes from ozō, the verb behind Martha’s warning at the tomb: by this time there is a stench. Five New Testament verses use it. Paul uses it for the aroma of the knowledge of Christ, and twice for an offering that pleases God.

In a few days one family went from the smell of death to the smell of nard. So the work of Christ gets out. Paul says God reveals through us the sweet aroma of his knowledge in every place, and he roots it in the cross: Christ gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance.

The dust says faith is a private matter, best kept quiet at home. But the fragrance filled the house. The sacrifice that pleased God was Christ’s, not yours, and it is His aroma that gets into the rooms where you live.
stations.live: This week, let one person in your house hear you thank Christ out loud for something specific He has done for you. Not a speech. One plain sentence, at supper, where they can hear it.

stations.verse: Now he said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the money box, used to steal what was put into it.
stations.question: Judas sat near Jesus and spoke up for the poor, yet John says he was a thief; where am I using a reason that sounds good to cover what I am keeping back for myself?
stations.gloss: a box, a chest; the money box
body: In older Greek, glōssokomon named a case for the reeds of musical instruments; here it is a box or chest. In the Greek Old Testament it is the chest King Joash set outside at the gate of Yahweh’s house for the people’s money. In the New Testament it appears in two verses, both in John, both about Judas.

The chest at the temple gate was filled by people who gave gladly. Judas held a box and emptied it into his own hands. When he later walked out to betray Jesus, the others thought he went to buy for the feast or give something to the poor.

The dust tells you your box is small and your reasons are good. Christ is not fooled by either. He knows what is in the box. The answer is not a better excuse. It is to bring the box to the One who was about to be betrayed by the man holding it, and to die for thieves.
stations.live: Find the one place where money talks to you in secret — the account no one sees, the spending you never name. Open it to your wife or a trusted brother this week. Say: ‘There is no box Christ doesn’t know about.’

stations.verse: But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. She has kept this for the day of my burial.
stations.question: Jesus silenced the complaint over Mary’s gift with Leave her alone and tied it to the day of my burial; what changes in my giving when I measure it by His burial for me rather than by what others think of it?
stations.gloss: preparation for burial
body: Entaphiasmos means preparation for burial. It comes from the verb entaphiazō and the New Testament has it in two verses, both words of Jesus at Bethany about this ointment. Days later Nicodemus would bring a mixture of myrrh and aloes for the same body.

Mark records Jesus saying she has anointed my body beforehand for the burying. John gives it this way: She has kept this for the day of my burial. Either way, Jesus turns a supper in His honor toward His grave. He speaks of His burial over a meal, six days out, like a man speaking of work he came to do.

The dust says your love for Christ is a waste and your gifts too small to matter. Jesus says, Leave her alone. He receives what is given and sets it beside His own death. What gives your offering its worth is the burial it answers — the grave He went into for you, and walked out of.
stations.live: Read John 19:38–20:18 slowly this week. Then do one quiet thing in His honor that no one will praise you for, and say: ‘This is for the One who was buried for me.’

practices.title: SIT AT THE TABLE FIRST
practices.body: Lazarus did not serve the supper. He sat at the table with Jesus. Before you do one thing for Christ this week, sit with Him. Read John 12:1–11 on three mornings, and before you ask Him for anything, thank Him by name for one grace He gave you before you had anything to offer. Let the serving come out of the sitting, and not the other way around.

practices.title: POUR OUT ONE COSTLY THING
practices.body: Mary gave a full pound, not a sample. Pick one thing this week that costs you — money given quietly to your church or a family in need, a Saturday spent on someone who cannot pay you back, the hour you guard hardest. Give it whole. Do not announce it. Give it because He gave His life first, and let it be an answer, not an investment.

practices.title: NAME YOUR BOX
practices.body: Judas kept a money box and stole from it while he sat near Jesus. Most men have some box: the account, the side deal, the habit paid for in cash. Sit down this week and write out where your money went last month. Bring the list to Christ before you bring it to anyone else. Then tell one brother the truth about it, and let the light in.

practices.title: LET THE FRAGRANCE OUT
practices.body: The fragrance filled the house, and no one missed it. Your love for Christ should not be a secret your children have to guess at. At supper one night this week, read John 12:1–3 aloud and say one plain sentence about what Christ has done for you. Keep it short. It will feel strange the first time. Your house will notice anyway.

practices.title: LIVE AS A RAISED MAN
practices.body: Many believed in Jesus because Lazarus was alive. He did not need to preach; the chief priests wanted him dead because his life pointed straight at Jesus. Yours does too, if Christ has raised you. This week, when someone asks how you keep going, tell him about the One who was buried for you and walked out of the tomb. One sentence is enough.

title: Ointment Poured Out
subtitle: from dust to love that spends everything
keyVerse: Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.

passage.text: Then six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, who had been dead, whom he raised from the dead.
So they made him a supper there. Martha served, but Lazarus was one of those who sat at the table with him.
Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.
Then Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, one of his disciples, who would betray him, said,
“Why wasn’t this ointment sold for three hundred denarii, and given to the poor?”
Now he said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the money box, used to steal what was put into it.
But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. She has kept this for the day of my burial.
For you always have the poor with you, but you don’t always have me.”
A large crowd therefore of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came, not for Jesus’ sake only, but that they might see Lazarus also, whom he had raised from the dead.
But the chief priests conspired to put Lazarus to death also,
because on account of him many of the Jews went away and believed in Jesus.

stationsIntro: Read each verse slowly, the way you would read a will that names you. Then answer plainly, and let the Greek word bring you back to the supper at Bethany and the One whose feet Mary anointed.
lifeIntro: Lazarus was already at the table when Mary broke open the nard. Christ had called him out of the grave before anyone in that house had a thing to give. None of what follows buys His favor; it is what a man does once he knows whose voice called him out.
lifePulls: Judas counted three hundred denarii. Mary counted her brother at the table. To the man keeping the box, love for Christ will always look like waste. To the man Christ has raised, it looks like the least he can do.
prayer: Father, Your Son went to a grave at Bethany and called the dead man out. Thank You that I was dead in my sin, and Christ called me out by name. Thank You that I sit at His table because He invited me, not because I paid. Teach me to love Him the way Mary did, with nothing held back. Show me the box I have kept for myself, and give me grace to open it. Forgive me for calling love for Jesus a waste and calling my own comfort wise. Fill my house with the fragrance of Christ, so my family knows who I love. Keep my eyes on His burial and His rising until I see Him face to face. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, Your Son went to a grave at Bethany and called the dead man out.
Thank You that I was dead in my sin, and Christ called me out by name.
Thank You that I sit at His table because He invited me, not because I paid.
Teach me to love Him the way Mary did, with nothing held back.
Show me the box I have kept for myself, and give me grace to open it.
Forgive me for calling love for Jesus a waste and calling my own comfort wise.
Fill my house with the fragrance of Christ, so my family knows who I love.
Keep my eyes on His burial and His rising until I see Him face to face.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Six days before His death, Jesus sat at a table with a man He had raised from the dead. Mary poured a pound of pure nard on His feet, and the house was filled with the fragrance. Judas called it waste because he was a thief with a box. Jesus called it preparation for His burial. Christ gave first. Love answers. Stop keeping the box, and pour out what you have on Him.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the table at Bethany. Look at the man sitting there who lay four days in the ground. Look at his sister on the floor with an empty jar and her hair wet with nard. Look at the house that smelled of death a week ago and now smells of something costly poured out. And look at the One in the middle of the room, who brought the dead man home and is about to go into a grave Himself.

The dust has told you to count. Keep your love for God within reason, it says. Give what is sensible, guard the rest, and keep a box for yourself where no one checks. Or it tells you the opposite — that you must keep paying in, because God has not made up His mind about you yet, and one more lean month will prove it. The first voice sat at that supper in one man. He counted three hundred denarii to the coin and missed the Son of God sitting a few feet away, the One who had just emptied a grave.

But Jesus did not count the cost of you. He walked toward the grave knowing what it held. He took Mary’s ointment and spoke of His burial, and within the week He was laid in a new tomb in a garden, wrapped in linen with about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes. He did not go in to get your love. He went in to give you His life. The body Mary anointed for burial did not stay buried. The grave He was anointed for is empty.

That is what you carry into Tuesday. Lazarus ate at that table because Christ had called his name at the tomb, and you sit at it for the same reason. Christ has already been buried for you, and He has already come out. Nothing you pour on Him is wasted, because nothing you give Him is a payment. It is an answer to a debt He already settled. When you open your hands this week — the money, the time, the truth about your box — you are doing what Mary did. You are loving a Savior who loved you first, at a table He set, in a house He filled with life.
closingVerse: Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.
carry: Mary poured a pound of pure nard on the feet of the One who had just given her brother back; what will you pour out at His feet this week in answer to what He has already given you?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust teaches a man to hold on. Grip the paycheck. Grip the name you have made. Grip the house, the health, the years you have left, and do not let any of it go into the ground. A sack of seed on the barn shelf looks safe. It is whole and dry and yours, and no frost can touch it there. The dust calls that life — keeping what you have from ever being buried.

And the dust wants a king who will help you keep it. A Jesus who clears the road, settles the debt, quiets the doctor, and leaves the rest of your life alone. You will shout for that king. You will wave branches for him. And when he turns toward a cross instead of a throne, you will wonder what went wrong, and why he did not keep his end.

A man who lives that way ends up gripping a handful of dry seed and calling it a harvest. He keeps everything and grows nothing. His marriage gets what is left after he has protected himself. His church gets his name on the roll. His God gets a request list. That man needs the psalm more than he needs a better grip: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)

The word that revives here is a farmer’s word, and Jesus says it about Himself before He says it about you. Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. The King rides in on a young donkey to be buried like seed, and the harvest is men from every nation who will live because He died.

sections.heading: The Next Day, at the Feast
pulls: The crowd wanted a King who would keep them out of the grave. Jesus came as a King who would go into it — a grain of wheat dropped in the ground so that He would not remain alone.
paras: The supper at Bethany is behind Him. On the next day a great multitude had come to the feast. Word about Lazarus has gone ahead of Jesus. The crowd that stood at the tomb was testifying about it, and a second crowd pours out of the city to meet the man who had done this sign. The chief priests are plotting to kill Him, and now Lazarus with Him. The Passover is days away, and the Lamb of God is walking toward it on purpose.

John packs a great deal into fifteen verses: the palm branches, the shout from the psalm, a young donkey and a prophet’s word, Pharisees who think they are losing, Greeks asking for Jesus, and then a saying about wheat that Jesus gives as His answer to all of it. Read 12:12–26 in one sitting, out loud if you can, and let the scene move at its own speed. Notice how John tells you the disciples did not understand until later, and notice when later was. It was after the empty tomb, and that is where this week will take you.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: BRANCHES AND A SHOUT
paras: Word moves fast at a feast. When they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, the crowd did not wait in the city. They took the branches of the palm trees and went out to meet him. A few days earlier men in the temple had been asking whether He would come at all. Now they walked out the road to bring Him in.

Then the shout. Hosanna, they cried, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel. The heart of that cry is a psalm of Israel: Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh’s name. One verse earlier in the same psalm is a plea: Save us now, we beg you, Yahweh. They hailed Him with the songs of their own Scriptures, and they gave Him the title Nathanael gave Him back in chapter 1: King of Israel.

Every word of it was true. He is the King. He does come in the name of the Lord. He has come to save. And yet before the week was out, the same city would hear its chief priests say, We have no king but Caesar. A crowd can shout the right words and still want a different King. Back in Galilee a crowd had tried to take him by force to make him king, and He had gone up the mountain alone.

You know that crowd. You have sung the right words on Sunday and wanted a Jesus who would mostly leave your Monday alone — bless the work, heal the knee, keep the bank off your back. He comes anyway. He does not wait for you to understand Him before He rides in.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: LOWLY, ON A YOUNG DONKEY
paras: Jesus, having found a young donkey, sat on it. John does not dress the moment up. No war horse, no chariot, no armed guard. A King on a young donkey, His feet near the dirt. And John tells you why: As it is written, Don’t be afraid, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey’s colt.

The words come from Zechariah, who said it in full: He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey. Mark the order. Righteous first — there is nothing crooked in this King. Then having salvation — He brings it with Him; He does not wait for you to bring something to Him. Then lowly. The King who has every right to come crushing comes riding low.

That is why the word John quotes opens with Don’t be afraid. A man with a guilty conscience has every reason to fear a righteous King. He has no reason to fear this one, because this King has come to carry the guilt, not to collect on it. Zechariah says He will speak peace to the nations. His war is won without a sword, and the peace He speaks reaches the man who has been at war with Him.

Then John makes a confession for himself and the others. His disciples didn’t understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written about him. They walked beside the donkey and did not know what they were seeing. Only after the cross and the empty tomb did it come clear. Grace runs that way. He does the work first, and understanding follows.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE HOUR HAS COME
pulls: Jesus is the grain of wheat. He fell into the earth first, and alone, so that He would not remain alone. Every man who follows Him follows a Seed that has already broken the ground.
paras: The crowd from Lazarus’ grave kept talking, and the Pharisees heard it. See how you accomplish nothing. Behold, the world has gone after him. They meant it as a complaint, men who had spent a whole chapter trying to stop Him and failing. John sets it down because it was truer than they knew. In the next breath, the world shows up.

Now there were certain Greeks among those that went up to worship at the feast. Men from outside Israel find Philip and ask a plain thing: Sir, we want to see Jesus. Philip tells Andrew. Andrew and Philip tell Jesus. And Jesus answers in a way that seems at first not to answer at all. The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.

All through this Gospel the hour has been coming. At Cana He said, My hour has not yet come. At the feast in chapter 7 they tried to seize Him, and no one laid a hand on Him because his hour had not yet come. Now it has come, and it comes when the nations knock. Jesus told you He has other sheep to bring. The Greeks at the edge of the crowd are the first of them.

But mark what glory means here. Jesus is not about to be crowned in the city. He is about to be betrayed by one of His own, nailed to a cross between two other men, and laid in a new tomb, and He calls that His glory. The world measures glory by how high a man climbs. The Son of Man is glorified by how low He goes for others. The Greeks want to see Jesus. He will show Himself to them, and to you, through His dying. Then He explains it with a seed.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE SEED AND THE SERVANT
paras: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. Jesus speaks of Himself first. He is the grain. If He stays out of the ground — no cross, no tomb — He remains alone, the one righteous Man in a world of dust, and no one goes with Him. But He will not stay alone. He falls into the earth, is laid in a garden tomb, and comes up again, and the harvest is every man who believes in Him, from Israel and from the nations.

Only then does He turn to you. He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life. Jesus does not ask you to loathe yourself or despise the breath God gave you. He is telling you that the life you grip for yourself in this world is a life you lose, and the life you let go for His sake is kept — kept to eternal life. A man who never plants his seed loses it slowly, to mice and damp. The farmer who puts it in the ground looks like a man throwing it away, until the field comes up green.

If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there my servant will also be. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. Follow where? Into the ground, and out of it. The servant goes where the Master went. But the Master went first, and went alone, and carried the grave for you. You follow a Seed that has already broken the earth, and at the end of the road waits the Father’s own honor.

stations.verse: They took the branches of the palm trees and went out to meet him, and cried out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!
stations.question: The crowd went out with palm branches to hail the King of Israel, though within days He would be crowned with thorns; what kind of king have I wanted Jesus to be instead of the King He came to be?
stations.gloss: a palm branch
body: Baion is a palm branch. It is a rare word, used in only one verse of the New Testament — this one. The crowd cut the branches and carried them out the road to meet a King.

Branches wilt. Before the week was out, Jerusalem was crying for His death. The welcome on the road was real, and it was thin. Jesus rode on anyway, toward a cross the crowd did not see coming, because His love never hung on theirs.

The dust says Christ stays only as long as your praise stays green. But John later saw a great multitude, which no man could count, out of every nation, standing before the Lamb with palm branches in their hands. That crowd does not wilt. It stands there because the Lamb was slain and lives. Your welcome does not hold Him. His death holds you.
stations.live: Think of the last time your praise for Christ wilted because He did not do what you wanted. Name it to Him this week, and say: ‘You are the King I need, not the one I ordered.’

stations.verse: They took the branches of the palm trees and went out to meet him, and cried out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!
stations.question: The crowd cried Hosanna, the psalm’s plea to be saved, to the One who would save them by dying; where have I asked Jesus to save me and then resented the way He chose to do it?
stations.gloss: hosanna; a Hebrew plea carried into Greek
body: Hōsanna is a Hebrew cry carried over into Greek letters, built from two Hebrew words. The psalm the crowd drew on has the same cry, put into English as Save us now, we beg you, Yahweh. Five verses of the New Testament carry it, all on the road into Jerusalem or in the temple that week.

The crowd prayed rightly with their mouths. They asked to be saved, and they asked the right Person. What they did not see was how He would answer: not by throwing out Rome, but by bearing sin and being buried like seed.

The dust says that if Christ does not save you your way, He has not saved you at all. But the cry was heard. Every hōsanna on that road was answered at the cross and the empty tomb. When you cry to Him now, you are calling on a Savior who has already done the saving that matters most.
stations.live: Each morning this week, pray Psalm 118:25 in your own words. Then add the answer you already have: ‘Save me now, Lord. You already did, at the cross. Do it Your way today.’

stations.verse: Jesus, having found a young donkey, sat on it. As it is written, “Don’t be afraid, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey’s colt.
stations.question: John says the King came sitting on a donkey’s colt so that Zion would hear Don’t be afraid; what fear of God’s anger am I still carrying that this lowly King came to take away?
stations.gloss: a young donkey; a little donkey
body: Onarion is the small form of the common word for a donkey: a young donkey, a little one. It appears in only one New Testament verse. Zechariah’s prophecy had said as much: a colt, the foal of a donkey.

A King on a war horse comes to take a city. A King on a young donkey comes to make peace. Zechariah tied the two together: this King is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and He will speak peace to the nations. John says it happened just as it is written. The King came the way the prophet said He would come.

The dust tells you that God is coming for you with a sword in one hand and your record in the other. The young donkey says otherwise. Your King comes low, close to the ground you cling to, and the first word over His coming is Don’t be afraid. He has come to make peace, and He will pay for it Himself.
stations.live: Read Zechariah 9:9–10 aloud this week. When you catch yourself bracing for God’s anger, say it back to Him plainly: ‘My King came lowly, bringing salvation. I will not be afraid of Him.’

stations.verse: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
stations.question: When Greeks came asking to see Jesus, He answered with a grain that remains by itself alone unless it dies; where am I looking for a Jesus I can admire without needing His death for me?
stations.gloss: a grain; a single seed
body: Kokkos is a grain, a single seed. It occurs in seven New Testament verses. Most are the mustard seed in Jesus’ teaching, small at the sowing and large at the end. The last is Paul, writing about the resurrection: That which you sow, you don’t sow the body that will be, but a bare grain.

Jesus took that ordinary seed and laid His own death inside it. One grain kept in the hand stays one grain. One grain buried comes up as many. No one forced Him into the ground. He chose the earth and the grave so that men from every nation would rise with Him.

The dust says a buried thing is a lost thing. Paul answers that that which you yourself sow is not made alive unless it dies. The Seed was buried. The Seed came up. And because He did, your own grave is not the end of you. It is a sowing.
stations.live: Stand at a grave this week — a parent’s, a friend’s, or the one that will someday carry your name. Say over it: ‘Christ was sown first. He came up. So will everyone who is His.’

stations.verse: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
stations.question: Jesus said the grain of wheat that dies bears much fruit, and His people are that harvest; where am I still trying to grow my own standing with God instead of resting in what His death produced?
stations.gloss: wheat; grain
body: Sitos is wheat, the grain men make bread from. In the Greek Old Testament it most often stands for the Hebrew word for grain. Fourteen New Testament verses mention it: wheat in the barn, wheat among weeds, wheat sold by the measure.

John the Baptist said Christ would gather his wheat into the barn. On the night before the cross, Jesus told Peter that Satan had asked to sift you as wheat — but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. Wheat is what Christ keeps. It is what He prays over and what He brings in at harvest.

The dust says you have to grow yourself into something God will keep. But the Grain fell first. The harvest comes out of His death, not your effort. You are wheat because He was buried, and He will gather His wheat into the barn at the last day. Not a grain of it will be lost.
stations.live: When you feel this week that your faith is about to give out, read Luke 22:31–32. Then say it: ‘He prayed for me. I am His wheat, and He will bring me in.’

practices.title: MEET THE KING HE IS
practices.body: The crowd waved branches for the King of Israel, and within days the city turned. Write down what you have been expecting Jesus to fix this year — the job, the body, the son who will not call. Bring that list to Him in prayer, then read Zechariah 9:9–10 over it. Ask Him to be the King He is, and to make you glad of the King He is.

practices.title: PRAY THE OLD CRY
practices.body: Hosanna was a plea for saving, and Christ answered it with His blood. Pray Psalm 118:25–26 each morning before work this week. Name one thing you need saving from today — the temper, the screen, the fear about money. Then thank Him that the great saving is already done, at the cross and the empty tomb. You are asking a Savior who has already answered, not a stranger who might.

practices.title: PUT ONE THING IN THE GROUND
practices.body: A grain that is never planted stays a single grain. Find one thing you have been holding to keep your life in this world safe — the savings you will not touch for anyone, the reputation you guard at any cost, the evenings you keep from your family. Let one of them go into the ground this week for Christ’s sake and someone else’s good. Do it because He went into the ground for you.

practices.title: GO WHERE HE IS
practices.body: Where I am, there my servant will also be. The Master went low, among the poor and the grieving and the dying. This week, go where He went: visit the man in the hospital, sit with the widow down the road, give an hour to the boy at church whose father left. You are not earning the Father’s honor. You are walking ground the Seed already walked.

practices.title: BRING ONE MAN TO JESUS
practices.body: The Greeks came saying, Sir, we want to see Jesus, and Philip and Andrew took the request straight to Him. Someone near you is asking the same thing in his own words — a coworker, a son, a neighbor at the feed store. Take him to Jesus this week the way Philip did: not with an argument, but by pointing him to the One who died and rose so that He would not remain alone.

title: Unless a Grain of Wheat Falls
subtitle: from dust to the harvest of a buried seed
keyVerse: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.

passage.text: On the next day a great multitude had come to the feast. When they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem,
they took the branches of the palm trees and went out to meet him, and cried out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!”
Jesus, having found a young donkey, sat on it. As it is written,
“Don’t be afraid, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey’s colt.”
His disciples didn’t understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written about him, and that they had done these things to him.
The multitude therefore that was with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead was testifying about it.
For this cause also the multitude went and met him, because they heard that he had done this sign.
The Pharisees therefore said among themselves, “See how you accomplish nothing. Behold, the world has gone after him.”
Now there were certain Greeks among those that went up to worship at the feast.
These, therefore, came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.”
Philip came and told Andrew, and in turn, Andrew came with Philip, and they told Jesus.
Jesus answered them, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.
Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life.
If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there my servant will also be. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.

stationsIntro: Read each verse out loud, slowly, as if you stood at the side of that road outside Jerusalem. Then answer the question plainly, and let the Greek word walk you back to the King on the young donkey and the Seed that went into the ground.
lifeIntro: The King has already come, lowly and bringing salvation. The Seed has already gone into the ground and come up again, and the harvest is already being gathered. These five practices follow a Savior who went first. None of them is the price of following Him; each is a way of walking behind Him this week.
lifePulls: The life you grip to keep is the life you lose. The life you let go into Christ’s hands is kept to eternal life — because He let His own go into the ground first.
prayer: Father, You sent Your Son into Jerusalem lowly, riding on a young donkey. Thank You that my King came righteous and bringing salvation, not a sword. Thank You that Jesus fell into the earth like a grain of wheat and did not stay there. Forgive me for wanting a king who only fixes my week and leaves my heart alone. Teach me to let go of the life I hold so tight, and to trust it to Your hands. Where Jesus is, let me be, among the people He loves. Gather men from every nation into the harvest of His death, and my neighbors among them. Keep me as His wheat until the day He brings me in. In Jesus’ name, amen.
