bottomLine: The crowd wanted a King who would keep them out of the grave. Jesus rode in on a young donkey, lowly and bringing salvation, to go into it. He is the grain of wheat that fell into the earth and died so that He would not remain alone, and the harvest is every man who believes in Him. Let go of the life you are holding on to. Follow the Seed that has already come up.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and see the branches lying in the road outside Jerusalem. Hear the old cry from the psalm go up from the crowd. See the King come over the rise, not on a war horse but on a young donkey, righteous and bringing salvation, low enough to touch. See Him ride past all that shouting toward a week that will end with a cross and a tomb in a garden.

The dust has told you to hold on. Keep the seed dry. Keep your life in the sack where nothing can bury it, and want a king who will keep it there with you. That crowd wanted a King too, and when He turned toward the ground, their welcome did not hold. The dust promised you a harvest and left you holding seed you were too afraid to plant. It has kept you safe from loss and starved you of fruit, and it calls that wisdom.

But your King did not keep His life. He spent it. He fell into the earth like a grain of wheat — betrayed, crucified, wrapped in linen, laid in a new tomb where no one had ever lain. He went in alone so that He would not remain alone. And early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, the ground gave Him back. The Seed came up, and He did not come up by Himself. Every man who believes in Him is the much fruit of His burial — men from Israel and from the nations, Greeks who asked to see Him, and you.

That is what you carry into Tuesday. Christ has already gone into the ground for you and come out. So the things you let go for His sake this week are not thrown away. They are sown. The hour you give, the grudge you drop, the money you let go of, the pride you let die — none of it is lost. The life you stop gripping is kept to eternal life, and where He is, there His servant will be. The Father Himself will honor the man who follows His Son. That man need not be the strongest hand in the field. He only needs to belong to the Seed.
closingVerse: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
carry: Jesus fell into the earth like a grain of wheat and came up bearing much fruit; since He went into the ground first, what will you let go of this week for His sake, trusting it is sown and not lost?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man learns early what gets a man lifted. You get lifted for the bid you won, the crew you held together, the year nobody got hurt. You get lifted by a handshake at the feed store and a good word passed along behind your back. It cuts the other way too. One bad season, one rumor, one thing said at the wrong table, and a man is pulled down. So you learn to watch your name the way a farmer watches the sky in August.

The dust takes that habit and builds a religion on it. It tells you the only height that counts is the height other men give you. It tells you a man nailed to a beam in public has lost — lost his name, lost his argument, lost his God. And it tells you that if you mean to get near God at all, you will have to haul yourself up to Him, one good week at a time, with men watching.

Live under that long enough and you stop expecting anything from heaven but a grade. The old prayer fits the floor you are lying on: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The man who first prayed it did not ask to be lifted by other men. He asked for a word, and he trusted the word to do the lifting.

John 12 gives that word. Jesus says the height that matters is a cross, and that from it He will pull men to Himself. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself. You do not climb to Him. He is lifted up, and you are drawn.

sections.heading: The Last Call to the Crowd
pulls: The dust says the height that counts is the height men give you. Jesus says the height that counts is a cross — and from there He draws to Himself men who could never have climbed to God.
paras: The Passover is days away. Jesus has ridden into Jerusalem on a young donkey, and some Greeks who came up to worship at the feast have gone to Philip and said, Sir, we want to see Jesus. Jesus answered by speaking of His own death. The time had come for the Son of Man to be glorified, and the grain of wheat must fall into the earth. Now He turns toward that death with His soul troubled, and He does not turn away from it.

This is the last stretch of His public teaching in John’s Gospel. After verse 36 He departed and hid himself from them, and from chapter 13 on He speaks to His own. So John stops the story, looks back over all the signs, and asks why so many who saw them did not believe. His answer comes out of Isaiah. Then Jesus cries out one more time to whoever will listen. Read 12:27–50 straight through before you go on, and listen for the words lifted up.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: A TROUBLED SOUL
paras: Now my soul is troubled. What shall I say? Do not hurry past that. The Son of God, who has just called a man four days dead out of his tomb, stands in the open and says His soul is troubled. He is not acting. The Word became flesh, and flesh shrinks from death. Jesus feels the weight of what is coming before a single nail is driven.

Then listen to what He does with the dread. He names the prayer He could pray — Father, save me from this time? — and He sets it down. But I came to this time for this cause. He did not stumble into this week. He came for it. So He prays the other prayer: Father, glorify your name. He wants His Father’s name made great more than He wants His own life spared. That is obedience with the whole cost counted, and He offered it in your place.

The Father answers out loud. I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again. The crowd heard something. Some said that it had thundered. Others said, An angel has spoken to him. Jesus tells them plainly whom the voice was for: This voice hasn’t come for my sake, but for your sakes. The Son did not need convincing. They did. The Father spoke from the sky so that men standing in the street would know the coming death was His own work, with His name set on it.

You have heard that voice too, only written down. God has spoken about His Son in this book, plainly and on purpose. What you do with it this week is the whole matter. Some men hear the Father and call it thunder.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: LIFTED UP FROM THE EARTH
paras: Now is the judgment of this world. Now the prince of this world will be cast out. Twice Jesus says now. The cross is a verdict on the world about to kill Him, and an eviction served on the prince who has held men by the fear of death. On the day the nails went in, the prince looked like the winner. He was the one being put out.

And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself. John does not leave you guessing what that means: he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die. Lifted up is the cross. Jesus had told Nicodemus: even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, as Moses lifted the bronze serpent on a pole, and the bitten man who looked at it lived. The pole was the cure. So is the cross.

And from the cross He draws. Not a few of one kind — all people. Greeks had just come asking to see Him. Men of every nation and sort would be pulled to the lifted Son. This is not a promise that every man will be saved. Jesus has already said, No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. It is a promise that the drawing is real, that it reaches every kind of man, and that it does not fail.

The crowd could not fit it together. We have heard out of the law that the Christ remains forever. Jesus does not argue. He tells them the light will not stay on forever: While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become children of light. The light is on for you now.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THEY COULD NOT BELIEVE
pulls: They saw the signs and did not believe. If you see Christ for who He is, God opened eyes you could never have opened yourself — and that is a reason to kneel, not a reason to strut.
paras: John looks back over everything he has written — water made wine, the official’s son, the man at the pool, the loaves, the blind man washing at Siloam, Lazarus walking out of the tomb — and sets down a hard sentence. Though he had done so many signs before them, yet they didn’t believe in him. The signs were not too few or too faint. The men who saw them would not come.

Then John goes underneath their refusal. He quotes Isaiah twice. First: Lord, who has believed our report? To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? Isaiah asked that about the Servant who would be exalted and lifted up, and will be very high — and then despised by the very people He came to save. Second, John says flatly, For this cause they couldn’t believe, and quotes the word God gave Isaiah to carry: He has blinded their eyes and he hardened their heart.

Sit still under that. John does not soften it, and you should not either. They would not believe, and that refusal was their own guilt. They could not believe, and over it stood God’s own hand. John sets the two side by side and does not explain how they fit. He wants you to see that God is not wringing His hands over the world’s unbelief. Not one refusal has slipped out from under His rule. And if you believe, you did not manufacture your own sight.

Then comes the sentence that opens the whole passage: Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him. Isaiah saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and John says the glory Isaiah saw was Christ’s. The One on the throne in the temple and the One about to hang on a cross are the same Lord.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE PRAISE THAT KEEPS A MAN QUIET
paras: Nevertheless even many of the rulers believed in him. After Isaiah, that word nevertheless is a crack of light. Among the hard there were men God had opened. But they didn’t confess it, so that they wouldn’t be put out of the synagogue, and John gives the reason without dressing it up: they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.

You know that man. You may be that man. Quiet about Christ at the shop, at deer camp, at the family dinner where the jokes run a certain way. Not because you stopped believing, but because the good opinion of those men still feels like the height that counts. Shame will not cure that. A man shamed into speaking goes quiet again the minute the shame wears off. What cures it is a better praise, and Jesus tells you where it is found.

He cries out, His last open call to the crowd in this Gospel. Whoever believes in me, believes not in me, but in him who sent me. And then: He who sees me sees him who sent me. There is no getting to the Father around the Son. To see Jesus is to see the Father, and to trust Him is to trust the One who sent Him. I have come as a light into the world, that whoever believes in me may not remain in the darkness.

And He tells them what He came for. I came not to judge the world, but to save the world. Judgment is real — The word that I spoke will judge him in the last day — but judging is not the errand that brought Him. He came carrying His Father’s commandment, and He knows what is in it: I know that his commandment is eternal life. God has lifted up His Son. He is not waiting to see whether men will lift you.

stations.verse: Therefore the multitude who stood by and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.
stations.question: The Father answered His Son’s prayer to glorify His name, and the crowd said that it had thundered; what has God said plainly about the cross of His Son that I keep hearing as background noise?
stations.gloss: thunder
body: Brontē is the plain word for thunder. It stands in eleven verses of the New Testament, and most of them are in Revelation, where thunders come out of the throne with lightnings and sounds. In Mark, Jesus hangs the word on two of His own men: James and John, the Sons of Thunder.

Here the thunder was the Father’s voice. God answered His Son in words — I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again — and part of the crowd heard only weather. Their explanation let them go home the same men they were. That is how a man handles a word from God he would rather not hear. He calls it noise.

The dust wants you to file every word of God under weather: loud for a moment, then gone. But Jesus said the voice came for your sakes. God did not speak to fill the sky. He spoke so men would know the cross was His work. That voice is still for you.
stations.live: Read John 12:27–30 aloud each morning this week. When you reach the Father’s answer, stop and say: ‘This voice came for my sake. I will not call it thunder.’

stations.verse: Now is the judgment of this world. Now the prince of this world will be cast out.
stations.question: Jesus said that in His death the prince of this world will be cast out; where am I still taking orders from a ruler the cross has already thrown out?
stations.gloss: to drive out, cast out, expel
body: Ekballō means to drive out, to cast or send out, to expel. It stands in seventy-five verses of the New Testament. John uses it for Jesus clearing the temple, for the Pharisees who threw him out — the man born blind — and here for the prince of this world.

Watch who gets thrown out in John and who does not. The religious men put the healed beggar out, and Jesus went looking for him. At the cross the prince is put out. And the man who comes to Christ hears the opposite word: He who comes to me I will in no way throw out. Same verb. Satan is cast out so that you never will be.

The dust says the accuser still runs your house, and that one day God will tire of you and show you the door. Christ answers with His cross. The accuser has been thrown out. You are inside with the Son.
stations.live: When the old accusation comes this week, do not argue from your record. Say out loud: ‘The prince of this world was cast out at the cross. Christ will in no way throw me out.’

stations.verse: And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.
stations.question: Greeks had just come asking to see Jesus, and He answered that once lifted up from the earth on the cross He would draw all people to Himself; whom have I quietly decided the cross could never reach?
stations.gloss: to lift up, raise high; to exalt
body: Hypsoō means to lift or raise up, and from there to exalt. Sixteen verses of the New Testament carry it. John has it in four, and every one is about the Son of Man being lifted up. Acts uses it of God exalting Jesus after He rose.

John lets you hear both senses at once. The lifting up is the cross — he says so in the next verse — and the cross is also where the Son is glorified. The pole that looked like shame was the place of His exaltation. And from there He draws men of every kind, not one nation only.

The dust says no man gets near God unless he lifts himself — his name, his effort, his good weeks. Hypsoō puts the lifting where it belongs. Christ was lifted up, and you were drawn. The man you wrote off is not out of reach of that pull.
stations.live: Write down the name of the man you have most quietly written off. Pray for him by name every morning this week: ‘You were lifted up to draw all kinds of men. Draw him, as You drew me.’

stations.verse: He has blinded their eyes and he hardened their heart, lest they should see with their eyes, and perceive with their heart, and would turn, and I would heal them.
stations.question: Though Jesus had done so many signs before them, John says they could not believe, because God has blinded their eyes; if I see Jesus for who He is, what pride in my own good sense does that take from me?
stations.gloss: to blind, make blind
body: Typhloō means to blind, to make blind. In the New Testament it is used only in a figure, of the mind rather than the eye of the body, in three verses: here, in Paul’s word that the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, and in John’s letter, where hatred of a brother leaves a man in the dark because the darkness has blinded his eyes.
Isaiah’s word stands behind this verse. Men watched Jesus open a blind man’s eyes, and their own stayed shut. John says God had blinded them. Sight of Christ is a gift.

The dust wants you to think you believe because you were smarter, or softer, or more honest than the men who walked away. If you see the glory of Christ, God opened your eyes. Thank Him, and keep praying for the blind.
stations.live: Tell one person this week, in plain words, how you came to believe. Give the credit where John gives it: ‘I did not find my own way to Christ. God opened my eyes.’

stations.verse: He has blinded their eyes and he hardened their heart, lest they should see with their eyes, and perceive with their heart, and would turn, and I would heal them.
stations.question: Isaiah’s word says God hardened their heart, so they would not turn and be healed, while Jesus still pleaded, While you have the light, believe in the light; what word of His have I heard for years without turning to Him?
stations.gloss: to harden; to make hard as stone
body: Pōroō comes from a word for a stone, and for the hard callus that forms on skin. It means to petrify, to harden. Its five New Testament verses all use it in a figure. Mark twice uses it of the Twelve: after the loaves their hearts were hardened, and Jesus asked them, Is your heart still hardened?

Isaiah’s word puts God’s hand on the hardening. Jesus’ word puts the warning in your ear: Walk while you have the light, that darkness doesn’t overtake you. A callus forms where the same rope rubs the same palm until the hand stops feeling it. A man can hear a true word so often that it stops reaching him.

But look at Mark again. The disciples had hard hearts too, and Jesus did not leave them. The dust says a hard heart is a closed case. God says, I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh. He is still speaking to you.
stations.live: Pick the word of Christ you have heard most often and felt least. Read it slowly every morning this week, then pray: ‘You take away the stony heart. Take mine.’

practices.title: LOOK AT THE CROSS FIRST
practices.body: Jesus said He would draw all people to Himself when He was lifted up, and John tells you He meant the cross. Before you pick up the phone each morning this week, read John 12:32–33 and put your eyes on the cross before you put them on anything else. Do not try to work up a feeling. Look where God put His Son. A man held by that pull will be pulled less by smaller things.

practices.title: SAY HIS NAME WHERE IT COSTS
practices.body: The rulers believed and kept quiet, because they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise. Name the room where you go silent about Christ — the break room, the hunting cabin, your brother-in-law’s porch. This week, say one plain, true thing about Jesus in that room. No sermon. Just let it be known whose you are. In Christ you already stand in the Father’s favor, so you can afford to lose a little of theirs.

practices.title: WALK WHILE THE LIGHT IS ON
practices.body: Jesus said, Walk while you have the light, that darkness doesn’t overtake you. There is a word from Him you have been putting off — an apology you owe your wife, a habit He has named, a call you keep not making. Do it this week. Do not wait until you feel ready. The light was given to walk in, and the Son who gave it went to the cross for every hour you sat in the dark.

practices.title: STOP CLIMBING
practices.body: Each time you see a cross this week — on a steeple, on a grave by the road, on a chain around someone’s neck — say it to yourself: ‘He was lifted up, and I was drawn.’ Then notice where you have been climbing for a better standing with God or with men: the extra hours to be seen, the story told to look good. Set one of those down by Friday. You were drawn. You do not need to climb.

practices.title: LET HIS WORD HAVE THE LAST SAY
practices.body: Jesus said the word He spoke will judge in the last day, and that the Father’s commandment is eternal life. Pick one evening this week and read John 12:44–50 with your wife or children, or alone if you live alone. Ask one question: what did Jesus say He came to do? Let His own answer stand — I came not to judge the world, but to save the world. Go to bed on that.

title: Lifted Up
subtitle: from dust to the cross that draws all men
keyVerse: And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.

passage.text: “Now my soul is troubled. What shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this time?’ But I came to this time for this cause.
Father, glorify your name!” Then a voice came out of the sky, saying, “I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.”
Therefore the multitude who stood by and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”
Jesus answered, “This voice hasn’t come for my sake, but for your sakes.
Now is the judgment of this world. Now the prince of this world will be cast out.
And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”
But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die.
The multitude answered him, “We have heard out of the law that the Christ remains forever. How do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up?’ Who is this Son of Man?”

Jesus therefore said to them, “Yet a little while the light is with you. Walk while you have the light, that darkness doesn’t overtake you. He who walks in the darkness doesn’t know where he is going.
While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become children of light.” Jesus said these things, and he departed and hid himself from them.
But though he had done so many signs before them, yet they didn’t believe in him,
that the word of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spoke, “Lord, who has believed our report? To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”
For this cause they couldn’t believe, for Isaiah said again,
“He has blinded their eyes and he hardened their heart, lest they should see with their eyes, and perceive with their heart, and would turn, and I would heal them.”
Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him.
Nevertheless even many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they didn’t confess it, so that they wouldn’t be put out of the synagogue,
for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.
Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me, believes not in me, but in him who sent me.
He who sees me sees him who sent me.
I have come as a light into the world, that whoever believes in me may not remain in the darkness.
If anyone listens to my sayings, and doesn’t believe, I don’t judge him. For I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.
He who rejects me, and doesn’t receive my sayings, has one who judges him. The word that I spoke will judge him in the last day.
For I spoke not from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.
I know that his commandment is eternal life. The things therefore which I speak, even as the Father has said to me, so I speak.”

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE CROSS LIFTED UP
stationsIntro: Read each verse aloud before you answer anything, the way a man reads a verdict handed down in his favor. Then write your answer plainly, and let the Greek word walk you back to the Son who was lifted up on the cross.
lifeIntro: The Son has been lifted up, the prince of this world has been thrown out, and the Father has spoken out loud from the sky. Everything below starts there. None of it earns a hearing with God; it is what a drawn man does once he knows who drew him.
lifePulls: Christ was lifted up on a cross so that you would never again need men to lift you. The praise you have been working for is small beside the voice the Father has already spoken over His Son.
prayer: Father, You glorified Your name in the death of Your Son, and You will glorify it again. Thank You that Jesus did not ask to be saved from that hour, but went into it for me. Thank You that He was lifted up on the cross, and that the prince of this world was thrown out. Thank You for drawing me when I could not come, and for opening eyes I could not open. Forgive me for loving the praise of men more than Your praise, and for the silence it has bought. Soften every hard place in my heart while You are still speaking to me. Draw the men I love who cannot yet see, as You drew me. Let me walk in the light this week and not sit down in the dark. In Jesus’ name, amen.

again.
Thank You that Jesus did not ask to be saved from that hour, but went into it for

Thank You that He was lifted up on the cross, and that the prince of this world
was thrown out.

Let me walk in the light this week and not sit down in the dark.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Jesus went to the cross with His soul troubled and His Father’s name on His lips. That lifting up was the judgment of the world, the casting out of its prince, and the drawing of men of every kind to the Son. Many saw the signs and could not see Him. If you see Him, God opened your eyes. Stop working for men’s praise. Walk while the light is on.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul. Look where God has lifted His Son. Look at Him with His soul troubled and His prayer unbroken: Father, glorify your name. Look at Him nailed up near the city, lifted from the earth and not hiding from it. Look at Him drawing men to Himself from the place where the world thought He was finished. Look long enough, and you will see that He drew you too.

The dust has kept your eyes on smaller heights. You have worked for the nod from the men at the feed store and the good word passed behind your back. You have kept quiet about Christ where it might cost you a little standing. You have heard God speak and called it thunder. And the whole time the dust has told you that God sits above it all, waiting to see how high you can climb.

But God did not wait for you to climb. He sent His Son down into the dust, and then He let Him be lifted up on a cross, and there the judgment of this world fell and its prince was thrown out. The accuser who held your name was put outside. And the Lord who spoke that word also said this one: He who comes to me I will in no way throw out. Isaiah saw His glory high on a throne. You see the same glory on a cross, lifted up for you.

Carry that into Tuesday. When the old charge comes, remember that the prince who brings it has already been cast out. When the praise of men pulls at you, remember that the Father has spoken out loud over His Son, and you are in Him. When you look at a man who seems too hard to reach, remember that the lifted Son draws all kinds of men, and He drew you. You did not climb to Him. He was lifted up on the cross and drew you, and He has said He will in no way throw you out.
closingVerse: And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.
carry: Jesus said that, lifted up on the cross, He would draw all people to Himself; where are you still trying to climb your way up to God this week instead of resting in being drawn?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: There is a kind of man who will help anyone and let no one help him. He will pull your truck out of the ditch in sleet and refuse to let you buy him breakfast. He will sit up with your father at the hospital and never mention that his own scan came back wrong. Men admire him for it. He admires himself a little too. He calls it strength.

The dust loves that man, because it can keep him alone. It tells him that being served is a kind of weakness, and that a man who lets another kneel at his feet has given something up. It tells him he can clean himself well enough, and that what he cannot clean he can at least keep covered. And when he comes to God, it tells him to come the same way — boots wiped, hands full of something he did himself.

That man is face down and calling it standing. He is closer to the psalmist than he thinks: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) Dust is what the road leaves on a man’s feet. He cannot shrug it off by being tough. Someone has to wash it.

In John 13 the Lord of all gets up from supper, ties a towel around His waist, and kneels on the floor. Then He says to the one man who tries to stop Him, If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me. He does not ask you for clean feet first. He asks for your feet.

sections.heading: Supper on the Last Night
pulls: The dust tells you to come to God with clean boots and full hands. Christ gets down on the floor with a basin and tells you the only way to have a part with Him is to let Him wash you.
paras: The crowds are gone. At the end of chapter 12 Jesus departed and hid himself from them, and from here through chapter 17 John keeps you with the Twelve on the last night. It is before the feast of the Passover. Jesus knows his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father. Judas is at the table, and the devil has already done his work in Judas’ heart. Before the night is out, Jesus will cross the brook Kidron into a garden, and men will come for Him there with torches.

John shows you what Jesus did before he tells you what it means. Watch the hands first — the water, the basin, the towel — and then listen to the words. The washing is first something Christ does to you, and only after that something He shows you how to do for others. Get that order backward and you will turn the gospel into a list of chores. Read 13:1–20 through before you go on.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: LOVED TO THE END
paras: John turns the corner of his Gospel with a sentence about love. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. Not to the end of His patience. To the end — all the way, to the last breath and past it. The men at that table would be scattered before morning, every one to his own place, and the loudest of them would deny Him before the rooster crowed. Jesus knew it. He loved them to the end anyway.

Then John sets two things side by side. During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him — and in the same breath, Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God. The devil is busy. Jesus is not rattled. He knows where He came from, where He is going, and what is in His hands.

That is what makes the next verse so hard to take in. A man who knew everything had been put into his hands would grip something. He would take the head of the table and wait to be served. Jesus knew it all, and what His hands did next was reach for a towel. His greatness did not keep Him off the floor. It took Him there.

See that before you see anything else. The One who washes you is no hired servant with nothing better to do. He is the Lord with all authority, choosing to kneel. He did not wash their feet because He had run out of options. He washed them because He loved them, and He had settled on loving them all the way.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE TOWEL AND THE BASIN
paras: John slows down and gives you each motion. Jesus arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. There is no speech first. There is only the work of His hands.

These were men with dirty feet at a supper. The Son through whom all things were made took their dirt into His own hands. He went around the table one man at a time. The hands that had made mud for a blind man’s eyes and handed out the loaves on the hillside now held a dirty heel. John does not tell you how long it took. He tells you the Lord did it.

Do not turn this into a rite. Jesus is not founding a ceremony for the church calendar. He is showing, with a towel and a basin, what He is about to do in His body. The Son who laid aside his outer garments and knelt would soon be stripped and lifted up on a cross, and there He would give Himself to make men clean. The basin points to the cross. The stoop at the table is the shape of the whole stoop He made when He came.

Paul would later put it into words. Christ emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. John lets you watch it happen on a floor, with water and a towel, while the bread is still on the table.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: NO PART WITH ME
pulls: You were bathed once, all over, when Christ made you His. What you pick up on the road this week is dust on the feet. Bring it to Him. It does not undo the bath.
paras: Then He comes to Peter, and Peter will not have it. Lord, do you wash my feet? Jesus tells him he will understand later. Peter digs in: You will never wash my feet. John does not tell you what was in Peter’s heart, but you know what is in yours when you say the same thing to Christ. It sounds like reverence. Most days it is the old pride that would rather go without than be done for.

Jesus answers with the hardest sentence in the chapter: If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me. There is no having Christ without being washed by Christ. A man may admire Jesus, quote Him, work for Him, and still have no part with Him if he will not let Him do the washing. That is the gospel in a basin. You are saved by what He does to you, not by what you do for Him.

Peter swings the other way. Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head. Jesus steadies him: Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean. The man Christ washes is clean all over. Forgiven, declared righteous, made His — that washing is done once, and it never needs doing again. What he picks up walking through the week is dust on the feet, and that he brings back to Christ to be washed. He is still completely clean.
Then the sorrow: You are clean, but not all of you. John explains: he knew him who would betray him. Judas was at the table. A man can have his feet in the basin and still not be clean.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: AS I HAVE DONE TO YOU
paras: When He has finished, He puts His garment back on, sits down, and asks, Do you know what I have done to you? Then He tells them who knelt in front of them: You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am. The Lord did that.

Only after the washing does the word about example come. If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. And then: I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you. The order is everything. He does not hand them a towel and tell them to earn a seat. He washes them, and then He sends them to the floor. You serve because you were served.

This is a way of living. The low job at home nobody thanks you for. The hard word you swallow so another man can be heard. The night drive across the county to sit with a brother whose life is coming apart. A servant is not greater than his lord. If your Lord took the basin, no job in your house is beneath you, and blessed are you if you do them.

Then Jesus names the shadow at the table. I know whom I have chosen. Judas was no surprise. The Scripture had said, He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me. Jesus tells them ahead of time that when it happens, you may believe that I am he. Even the betrayal would prove who He is. And He sends the washed men out under His own name: he who receives me, receives him who sent me.

stations.verse: During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him.
stations.question: At that supper the devil had already put betrayal in Judas’ heart, yet Jesus, knowing all things were in His hands, rose to serve; when wrong is at work at my own table, where do I look for footing?
stations.gloss: the main meal of the day; dinner, supper
body: Deipnon is the chief meal of the day — dinner, supper. It is found in sixteen verses. John uses it for the supper at Bethany where Lazarus sat at the table, for this supper, and once more near the end of his book, when he recalls the disciple who had also leaned on Jesus’ breast at the supper.

A supper is where men sit close, pass bread, and let their guard down. That is where the betrayal sat. And that is where Jesus rose to serve. He did not leave the table because of Judas. He did not wait for a cleaner room. He served the meal He had, with the men He had.

The dust says a table is ruined once someone at it has turned on you. But the last supper in the Bible is not Judas’ supper. It is the wedding supper of the Lamb, and every man at that table has been washed. Christ is setting it now.
stations.live: Pick one supper this week and, before anyone eats, thank God out loud for each person at the table by name — the hardest one to love included. Then be the first to serve them.

stations.verse: Arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
stations.question: Jesus knew the Father had given all things into his hands, and He used those hands to tie on a towel; where am I using whatever authority I have at home to be served rather than to serve?
stations.gloss: a linen cloth; a towel
body: Lention is a linen cloth, a towel. The word came into Greek from Latin, and it appears in only two verses of the New Testament, back to back, both here. It is the towel Jesus tied around His waist, and it is the towel He wiped their feet with. Same cloth.

There is nothing holy about a towel. It hangs by the back door and goes in the wash with everything else. That is the point. The hands that held all things picked up the plainest thing in the room and tied it on like a work apron. He did not serve from a distance. He wore the cloth He worked with.

The dust says authority means you get to drop the towel for someone else to pick up. Christ shows you what authority is for. Every man who leads anyone — a crew, a household, a son — has been handed a towel by the One who wore it first.
stations.live: Find the job at home you always leave for someone else — the dishes, the bathroom, the laundry. Do it this week without being asked. While you do it, say: ‘My Lord tied on a towel first.’

stations.verse: Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
stations.question: The Lord who held all things poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet; what part of my life have I decided is too dirty for Him to stoop to?
stations.gloss: a basin for washing
body: Niptēr means a basin. It is built on the verb for washing a part of the body — hands, face, feet. It stands in one verse of the whole New Testament: this one. A common word for a common thing, used once, for the night the Lord of glory filled it.

The basin sits on the floor, and whoever holds it is lower than the man whose feet are in it. Jesus put Himself below every man at that table, and no one there had asked Him to. He was not playing at humility. He was showing them the shape of His whole coming. He came down from the Father, and He kept coming down, all the way to the cross.
The dust says that if God saw what your feet looked like, He would keep His distance. Christ fills the basin anyway. He has seen the worst of your road, and He kneels to it with water. Let Him.
stations.live: Read John 13:1–5 slowly each morning this week and stop at the basin. Think of whose hands are holding it. Then say: ‘The Lord of all knelt for men like me. I will stop keeping my distance.’

stations.verse: Jesus said to him, “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean. You are clean, but not all of you.
stations.question: Jesus told Peter, Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean; what sin from this week have I treated as though it undid the whole washing Christ gave me?
stations.gloss: to bathe; to wash the whole body
body: Louō means to bathe, to wash the whole body. It is found in five verses. Greek had another word for washing a part of you — hands, face, feet — and Jesus uses both in this one sentence. Hebrews uses louō for the man who draws near to God with our body washed with pure water.

That is the Christian life in a single verse. There is a bath that happens once. When Christ washes a man — forgives him, declares him righteous, makes him His own — he is clean all over, and it does not need doing again. Then there is the dust of the week: the short temper, the screen, the lie told to dodge a hard talk. That he brings back to be washed, again and again.

The dust works both sides. Some days it says one bad night proves you were never bathed. Other days it says you are bathed, so the feet do not matter. Christ answers both: You are clean. Now bring Him your feet.
stations.live: Each night this week, name to Christ the dust of that day, one thing at a time. Then end with His word, not your feelings: ‘I have been bathed. Wash my feet.’

stations.verse: I don’t speak concerning all of you. I know whom I have chosen. But that the Scripture may be fulfilled, ‘He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me.’
stations.question: Jesus named the coming betrayal from the psalm that when it happens, you may believe that I am he; what betrayal in my own life have I taken as proof that God had lost hold of things?
stations.gloss: the heel
body: Pterna is the heel. The New Testament has it once, here, where Jesus quotes the psalm. In the Greek Old Testament it stands for the Hebrew word for heel. To lift the heel against a man is to turn on him, and the psalm puts it on the lips of a man betrayed by my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me.

The psalm speaks of a friend in whom I trusted. Jesus quotes only the bread and the heel, and just before He quotes them He says, I know whom I have chosen. He was not fooled. He knelt and shared bread knowing exactly who would turn.

The dust says that when a friend turns on you, the floor has dropped out and God was caught napping. Christ told His men ahead of time so that the betrayal itself would steady their faith. Nothing that night took Him by surprise. Nothing in your week will either.
stations.live: Think of the man who has turned on you. Pray for him by name this week, then say: ‘Christ saw the heel coming and went to the cross anyway. He holds this too.’

practices.title: LET HIM WASH YOU
practices.body: Jesus said, If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me. Most men would rather serve than be served, and that pride walks straight into their prayers. This week, quit coming to God as if you had already cleaned up. Each morning, before you ask Him for anything, tell Him one plain thing that needs washing. Do not dress it up or explain it away. Let the Lord who knelt with a basin do what He came to do. He is not shocked by your feet.

practices.title: STOP ASKING FOR A NEW BATH
practices.body: Peter swung from You will never wash my feet to wanting his hands and head done too. Jesus told him he was completely clean. When you fall this week, do not treat it as though your salvation just came undone. Confess the sin by its name, thank Him that you were bathed once for all, and get back up. Keep short accounts, quickly settled, as a man who knows he is clean. Shame keeps a man away from the basin. Grace brings him back to it.

practices.title: TAKE THE LOWEST JOB
practices.body: Your Lord took up the towel with all things in His hands. Pick one job this week that sits below your pride — scrubbing the grill, clearing the gutters, hauling the trash nobody wants to touch, staying late to sweep up the job site. Do it without announcing it. A servant is not greater than his lord. If He knelt, there is no floor in your life too low for you. The blessing is in the doing.

practices.title: SERVE THE ONE WHO HURT YOU
practices.body: Jesus served a table where betrayal was already planned. Think of the person who has hurt you most this year and is still in your life — a brother, an in-law, a man on the crew. Find one practical way to serve him this week: a ride, a meal, a hand with his fence. Do not wait to feel warm toward him. You are not excusing what he did. You are doing what was done for you, when you were the one at fault.

practices.title: RECEIVE THE MEN HE SENDS
practices.body: Jesus said, he who receives whomever I send, receives me. Think of the man God has put in your path to bring you His word — your pastor, an older man at church, the brother who told you the truth when you did not want to hear it. This week, tell him plainly that what he said took hold. Thank him by name. Receiving the man Christ sends is part of receiving Christ, and through Him the Father who sent Him.

title: He Washed Their Feet
subtitle: from dust to the towel and the basin
keyVerse: Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.

passage.text: Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him,
Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God,
arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
Then he came to Simon Peter. He said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”
Jesus answered him, “You don’t know what I am doing now, but you will understand later.”
Peter said to him, “You will never wash my feet!” Jesus answered him, “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.”
Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!”
Jesus said to him, “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean. You are clean, but not all of you.”
For he knew him who would betray him, therefore he said, “You are not all clean.”
So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you?
You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.
Most certainly I tell you, a servant is not greater than his lord, neither is one who is sent greater than he who sent him.
If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.
I don’t speak concerning all of you. I know whom I have chosen. But that the Scripture may be fulfilled, ‘He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me.’
From now on, I tell you before it happens, that when it happens, you may believe that I am he.
Most certainly I tell you, he who receives whomever I send, receives me; and he who receives me, receives him who sent me.”

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE TOWEL AND THE BASIN
stationsIntro: Take these verses one at a time and read each aloud, slowly. Answer the question in a sentence or two, and let the Greek word bring you back under the hands of the Lord who knelt.
lifeIntro: This week is not about a basin in the church basement. Christ has already done the washing that matters: He knelt with the towel, and then He went to the cross to make you clean all over. What follows is what a washed man does with his hands. None of it buys you a cleaner standing with God; you already have one.
lifePulls: Christ did not hand His men a towel and tell them to earn a seat. He washed them first, then sent them to the floor. You serve because you have been served, and you kneel because He knelt.
prayer: Father, You gave all things into the hands of Your Son, and He used them to wash His friends’ feet. Thank You that He loved His own to the end, and that His love went all the way to the cross. Thank You that He has washed me, and that I am clean. Forgive me for the pride that would rather go without than be served by You. Wash the dust of this day off my feet; I bring it to You by name. Keep me from doubting the bath when I stumble, and from ignoring my feet when I stand. Give me hands that reach for the towel at home and at work. When someone turns on me, remind me that nothing surprised my Lord. Thank You that He told His friends ahead of time, so that when the worst came they would believe. In Jesus’ name, amen.
