bottomLine: Jesus knew all things were in His hands, and He used those hands to wash dirty feet. The towel and the basin point to the cross, where the Lord stooped all the way to make men clean. If He does not wash you, you have no part with Him. If He has, you are clean all over, and you bring Him the dust of each day. Then, washed, you pick up the towel for others.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and see who is kneeling at your feet. See the One into whose hands the Father gave all things. See Him lay aside His outer garments and tie a towel around His waist. See Him pour the water and go around the table, man by man, until He comes to you. He did not send a servant. He came Himself. See His hands on the dirt you would have hidden.

The dust told you to keep your feet under the table. It said a man who lets himself be served has given something up. It said you could clean yourself well enough, or at least cover what you could not clean. And when you fell again, it said the whole bath was off and you would have to start over. You have lived a long time on those lies, and they have left you tired and proud at once. A man cannot carry his own dust and his own pride for long.

But hear Him. If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me. He did not say it to shut Peter out. He said it to bring him in. The towel and the basin pointed to a deeper washing. Before long He was stripped of His garments and lifted up on a cross. A soldier pierced His side, and immediately blood and water came out. He gave Himself for men with dirty feet. That is the bath. It was given once, and it holds.

His own words go with you out the door this week: You are clean. Not because you kept yourself clean, but because He washed you. When the dust of the week sticks to you, bring Him your feet; He has not put the basin away. When the low job waits at home, pick up the towel; He wore it first. And when someone at your own table turns on you, remember that your Lord saw the heel coming, washed feet anyway, and went on to the cross for you. No one can take your part with Him.
closingVerse: Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
carry: The Lord knelt with a basin and said, If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me; what are you still keeping out of His hands this week because you would rather clean it yourself?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: You have made vows you meant. You stood at the front of a church and promised to love her until death. You held your first son and swore he would never hear from you what you heard from your father. You told a friend in a hospital hallway that you would be there, whatever it took. You meant every word, and you may even have kept some of them.

Then the dust gets hold of those vows and tells you a lie about love. It says love is a thing you produce — a promise held up by the grip of the man who made it. Mean it harder and you will hold. And when you do not hold, when the silence settles into the house or the old friend stops calling, the dust has a second word ready: you are a man who cannot love. Quit pretending. Keep your guard up and keep the peace by keeping out.

A man who believes that will either boast or hide, and both leave him face-down in the same ground. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The cure for a broken vow is not a louder vow. It is a word that comes from outside you and holds when you do not.

John 13 gives you that word at a supper table. One man walks out into the night. Another swears he will die for his Lord before morning. And between them Jesus gives a commandment measured not by their love but by His: Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.

sections.heading: One Long Night at the Table
pulls: The dust says love is a promise held up by the man who makes it. Jesus gives a commandment held up by the One who gives it — measured by His love, not by yours.
paras: The basin is still wet. Jesus has just washed the disciples’ feet, Judas’ among them, and told the men that a servant is not greater than his lord. John opened the scene with a sentence that governs everything after it: having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. Hold on to that line. The rest of this chapter will put weight on it.

From here to the close of chapter 16, John sets down one evening of words — the last long talk Jesus had with His own before the arrest. It opens with a traitor named and a boaster warned. John, who calls himself only the disciple whom Jesus loved, was at that table, close enough to lean against his Lord. He wrote it down so you would know what kind of love was in the room that night, and what kind of men it was spent on.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: ONE OF YOU
paras: When Jesus had said this, he was troubled in spirit. Read that slowly. The Son of God sat at supper with a man He knew would hand Him over, and it shook Him. He was not a statue at the head of the table. He felt the weight of what was coming, as He had felt it at Lazarus’ grave. Then He testified — He said it plainly, so no one could mistake it: Most certainly I tell you that one of you will betray me.

Watch the eleven. The disciples looked at one another, perplexed about whom he spoke. No one pointed at Judas. He had walked the same roads, eaten the same bread, carried the money box for all of them. His feet were as clean as theirs. From the outside, the man who would sell Jesus looked like every other man at the table.

Peter will not sit in the fog. He catches the eye of the disciple leaning against Jesus’ breast and signals him to ask. That disciple does the simplest thing in the room. He, leaning back, as he was, on Jesus’ breast, asked him, “Lord, who is it?” He does not guess. He does not whisper theories down the table. He asks the One who knows.

There is grace in that. The man nearest to Jesus was not there on his record. In his own book he never gives his name, only that he was loved. Nearness to Christ is not won at the table. It is given, and then it is used: you lean in, and you ask.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE MORSEL AND THE NIGHT
paras: Jesus answers with His hands. It is he to whom I will give this piece of bread when I have dipped it. Then He dips it and gives it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. A few verses earlier He had quoted the psalm: He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me. Now the Scripture is fulfilled in front of them. The last thing Judas took from Jesus was bread from His own hand.

After the piece of bread, then Satan entered into him. The devil had already put the betrayal into Judas’ heart; now he takes the man over. And it is Jesus, not Satan, who gives the order of the hour: What you do, do quickly. The traitor is not running this night. The Son is. He goes to the cross because He lays His life down, not because a thief got the better of Him.

Nobody at the table knew why he said this to him. Some thought Judas was off to buy for the feast or to give something to the poor. So he walks out with their good opinion still on him. Therefore having received that morsel, he went out immediately. It was night.

Three words, and John means you to feel them. Jesus had said, if a man walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light isn’t in him. Judas had walked beside the light of the world, and he walked away from it into the dark. Being at the table is not the same as belonging to the Lord of the table. That is the warning. The grace is that the Light did not go out. Eleven men stayed in the room, no better than Judas by nature, and they were kept.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: LOVE BY A NEW MEASURE
pulls: The old command measured love by how a man treats himself. The new one measures it by how Christ has treated you — the towel, the bread, the cross. It is given before it is ever asked for.
paras: The door closes, and Jesus speaks of glory. Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him. The arrest is near. The cross is close. And Jesus calls it glory. In this Gospel the cross is where the Son shows the Father most clearly — love that goes all the way down into death for men who have not earned it.

Then He turns to the eleven with the tenderest word in the chapter. Little children, I will be with you a little while longer. He is leaving. Where He is going, they cannot come yet. And before He goes, He leaves them a charge: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.

What is new about it? Love for a neighbor was written in the Law long before: you shall love your neighbor as yourself. The newness is in the measure. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another. The old command measured love by how a man treats himself. The new one measures it by how Christ has treated you — the towel, the basin, the bread handed to a traitor, and before another night falls, the cross. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.

Notice the order. As I have loved you comes before you also love. The love is given before it is asked for. You do not love your way into His favor. You love out of the love already poured on you. And He says it will be seen: By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. Not by your vocabulary. By how you treat the men in the next pew.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: WILL YOU LAY DOWN YOUR LIFE?
paras: Peter answers the part about leaving. Lord, where are you going? Jesus gives him a no and a yes. Where I am going, you can’t follow now, but you will follow afterwards. Not now. But afterward. Keep that word in your pocket. Peter is about to need it.

Then Peter makes his vow. Lord, why can’t I follow you now? I will lay down my life for you. Hours later he would draw a sword in a garden. But look at what he has said. He has offered to do for Jesus the very thing Jesus came to do for him. The Shepherd had already told them, The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. Peter has it backward. He thinks the sheep will die for the Shepherd.

Jesus hands the vow back to him. Will you lay down your life for me? Most certainly I tell you, the rooster won’t crow until you have denied me three times. Not once. Three times, before the sun is up. Jesus is not guessing, and He is not cruel. He tells Peter the truth about himself before Peter has to learn it in a courtyard, warming himself at a fire.

And still He does not send him out. He keeps Peter at the table, and in the next breath He says to him and to all of them, Don’t let your heart be troubled. This is the love of 13:1 holding under load. Jesus knew the denial was coming and loved Peter to the end anyway. Peter’s story is not over. You will follow afterwards is a promise, and the One who made it keeps His word. Your boast will fail. His love will not.

stations.verse: The disciples looked at one another, perplexed about whom he spoke.
stations.question: When Jesus said one of them would betray Him, the disciples looked at one another, perplexed about whom he spoke, since Judas looked like the rest; what am I counting on my outward record to prove, when only Christ sees my heart?
stations.gloss: to be at a loss; to be perplexed, without a way forward
body: Aporeō means to be at a loss — perplexed, with no way through. It is built on a word for a way or a means, with a negative in front. It stands in six verses of the New Testament. Luke uses it of the women at the empty tomb.

At the supper the eleven are at a loss in the same way. Jesus says one of you, and they have nothing to go on. They could not tell. Only Jesus knew, and He had known all along — and He still washed that man’s feet with the rest.

The dust says that when you are at a loss, you are lost — that a man without answers is a man without footing. But the One at the head of this table is never perplexed. Paul could write that he was perplexed, yet not to despair. You can run out of answers and still be held by the One who has every one of them.
stations.live: When you cannot read a situation this week — a man at work, your own son, your own heart — stop guessing out loud. Take it to Jesus by name and say: ‘Lord, You know what I do not.’

stations.verse: He, leaning back, as he was, on Jesus’ breast, asked him, “Lord, who is it?
stations.question: Peter beckoned to the disciple leaning against Jesus’ breast, and he simply asked, Lord, who is it?; what hard question about my own life have I been taking to everyone except Jesus Himself?
stations.gloss: the breast; a man’s chest
body: Stēthos is the plain word for a man’s chest. Five verses of the New Testament use it. Twice Luke uses it of men beating their breasts — the tax collector who would not lift his eyes, and the crowds going home from the cross. Twice John uses it of himself, leaning on the breast of Jesus.

John never forgot that night. Near the end of his Gospel, when Peter turns and sees him following, he names himself again as the one who had also leaned on Jesus’ breast at the supper. Of all the ways he could describe himself, he picks that one: the man who was close enough to ask.

The dust wants you to think closeness to Christ is a prize for the best men. But the breast a sinner beats in shame and the breast a disciple leans on share one word, and the tax collector went home justified. Nearness to Jesus is a gift. Lean in and ask.
stations.live: Pick the question about your life you have been chewing on alone. Each morning this week, put it to Him in plain words, the way that disciple did: ‘Lord, I am asking You.’

stations.verse: Jesus therefore answered, “It is he to whom I will give this piece of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the piece of bread, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
stations.question: Jesus handed the bread to Judas with His own hand, and Judas took it and went out immediately; where am I taking good things from Christ’s hand while my heart is turned away from Him?
stations.gloss: a morsel; a small piece of bread
body: Psōmion is a small word for a small thing: a bit, a morsel. It is a diminutive form, and in the whole New Testament it appears in three verses, all of them here. John says it when Jesus hands it over, when Satan enters, and when Judas walks out.

John keeps your eye on it because the psalm Jesus quoted said the betrayer would be a man who eats bread with me. Judas did. He took food from the hand of the One who had told the crowds, I am the bread of life. He held the morsel and missed the Bread.

The dust says being near the things of God is the same as having God — the pew, the table, the Bible on the dash. Judas had all of it. But Christ gives Himself to every man who comes to Him: Whoever comes to me will not be hungry. Take Him, not only His bread.
stations.live: Before the evening meal each night this week, say the words aloud over the table, even if only you hear them: ‘Jesus is the bread of life, and I have come to Him.’

stations.verse: Little children, I will be with you a little while longer. You will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you can’t come,’ so now I tell you.
stations.question: With Judas gone into the night, Jesus calls the eleven Little children and tells them He is going where they cannot come; what hard word of His do I need to hear in that tender voice?
stations.gloss: a little child; a word of tender address
body: Teknion is the small form of the ordinary word for a child: little child. In the New Testament it is always spoken to someone, always in the plural, always as a word of affection. Eight verses carry it — this one in John’s Gospel, and the other seven in his first letter.

Judas has just gone into the night. Jesus is about to tell the eleven that He is leaving and they cannot come. And the first word out of His mouth is Little children. John kept that word. In his letter he writes, I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven you for his name’s sake.

The dust says that when Jesus goes, you will be left on your own to fend for yourself. But hear the voice He uses for hard news. He does not speak to hired men. He speaks to children He means to keep, whose sins are forgiven for His name’s sake, not theirs.
stations.live: Read 1 John 2:1 and 2:12 aloud on the morning you feel least like a son. Then say it back to Him: ‘You call me Your little child, and my sins are forgiven for Your name’s sake.’

stations.verse: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
stations.question: Jesus gave the new commandment with His own love as its measure — Just as I have loved you, you also love one another; which brother in Christ have I been loving only as far as he deserves?
stations.gloss: a commandment; a charge given with authority
body: Entolē is a charge laid on someone, an order given with authority. The New Testament uses it for the commandments of God in the Law, and it stands in sixty verses. John uses it for the charge the Father gave the Son — I received this commandment from my Father — and here for the charge the Son gives His own.

Love one another was not new. What is new is the measure: Just as I have loved you. Jesus was carrying out a commandment of His own that night — to lay His life down and take it again. He does not lay on you a load He has not carried first.

The dust says a commandment is a weight you lift to win God’s approval. John answers that the new commandment is true in him and in you; because the darkness is passing away. It is true in Christ first. His love is the ground you stand on before it is the work you do.
stations.live: Name the brother you keep at arm’s length. This week do one plain thing for him that costs you something, and tell no one. Say it as you go: ‘As He loved me, so I will love him.’

practices.title: START WITH HIS LOVE
practices.body: The commandment begins with as I have loved you, so begin each morning there. Read John 13:1–17 one day and 13:31–38 the next, and keep going back to them all week. Before you pray about the people who wear you out, name one way Christ has loved you that you did not deserve — the washing, the bread, the cross. Love that is not fed by His love runs dry by Wednesday. His does not run dry.

practices.title: LOVE THE MAN IN THE NEXT PEW
practices.body: Jesus said everyone would know His disciples by their love for one another. Think of a man in your church you have quietly written off — the one who talks too much, or the one who hurt you. Do one concrete thing for him this week: a call, breakfast, a ride, a Saturday helping with a job on his place. You are not proving anything to anyone. You are passing on what was handed to you.

practices.title: STOOP AT HOME
practices.body: The measure of this love is the towel and the basin, and at home that looks small and specific. Find the chore you leave for your wife because you think it beneath you, and do it without being asked or thanked. Drop the side comment you make at supper. Put the phone face-down when your son wants to talk. This is what Christ’s kind of love looks like with your sleeves rolled up.

practices.title: TRADE THE VOW FOR A PRAYER
practices.body: Peter said, I will lay down my life for you, and he fell before the rooster crowed. Your big promises will go the same way. This week, stop promising God what you will do for Him, and ask Him to do what He has promised to do for you. Instead of ‘I will never again,’ pray, ‘Keep me, Lord, because I cannot keep myself.’ The strength is in His word, not yours.

practices.title: COME BACK THE SAME DAY
practices.body: Jesus told Peter he would deny Him, and in the same breath told him, you will follow afterwards. If you deny Christ this week — with your silence at work, with a laugh you should not have joined, with the old habit after dark — do not stay out in the night. Go back to Him that same day and name it plainly. The One who foretold the fall had already made a way back.

title: A New Commandment
subtitle: from dust to love as He has loved
keyVerse: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.

passage.text: When Jesus had said this, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, “Most certainly I tell you that one of you will betray me.”
The disciples looked at one another, perplexed about whom he spoke.
One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was at the table, leaning against Jesus’ breast.
Simon Peter therefore beckoned to him, and said to him, “Tell us who it is of whom he speaks.”
He, leaning back, as he was, on Jesus’ breast, asked him, “Lord, who is it?”
Jesus therefore answered, “It is he to whom I will give this piece of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the piece of bread, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
After the piece of bread, then Satan entered into him. Then Jesus said to him, “What you do, do quickly.”
Now nobody at the table knew why he said this to him.
For some thought, because Judas had the money box, that Jesus said to him, “Buy what things we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor.
Therefore having received that morsel, he went out immediately. It was night.
When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him.
If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and he will glorify him immediately.
Little children, I will be with you a little while longer. You will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you can’t come,’ so now I tell you.
A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”
Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered, “Where I am going, you can’t follow now, but you will follow afterwards.”
Peter said to him, “Lord, why can’t I follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”
Jesus answered him, “Will you lay down your life for me? Most certainly I tell you, the rooster won’t crow until you have denied me three times.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE NEW COMMANDMENT
stationsIntro: Read each verse with the whole supper in view — the basin, the bread, the open door, the rooster. Answer the question in plain words, then let the Greek word send you back to the One who loved His own to the end.
lifeIntro: Christ loved His own to the end — the eleven who would scatter and the one who would swear he never knew Him. He gave the new commandment with that love already spent on them. These five practices are what a man does once he has been loved like that; none of them is a way of earning it.
lifePulls: Jesus knew one man would sell Him and another would deny Him, and He loved them to the end anyway. That love is not the target you aim at. It is the place you start from.
prayer: Father, Your Son loved His own to the end, and He has loved me. Thank You that He knew Judas and still washed his feet, and that He knew Peter and did not cast him out. Thank You that He laid down His life for me before I could promise Him anything. Forgive me for the vows I made in my own strength and broke within the week. Forgive me for the cold distance I keep from brothers You have told me to love. Pour the love of Christ into me until it runs over toward them. Keep me from walking out into the night while I sit near Your table. When I fall, bring me back quickly, and let me follow Him afterward. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, Your Son loved His own to the end, and He has loved me.
Thank You that He knew Judas and still washed his feet, and that He knew Peter
and did not cast him out.
Thank You that He laid down His life for me before I could promise Him
anything.
Forgive me for the vows I made in my own strength and broke within the week.
Forgive me for the cold distance I keep from brothers You have told me to love.
Pour the love of Christ into me until it runs over toward them.
Keep me from walking out into the night while I sit near Your table.
When I fall, bring me back quickly, and let me follow Him afterward.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: At supper Jesus named a traitor, handed him bread, and let him go out into the night. Then He gave the eleven a commandment with a new measure: love one another as I have loved you. Peter swore he would die for Him, and Jesus told him the rooster would crow first. Your love will fail. His did not, and it is the ground your love stands on. Receive it first. Then pass it on.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul; the One at the head of the table is looking at you. He knew the man who would sell Him, and He washed his feet. He knew the man who would swear he had never met Him, and He kept him close. He knew every man in that room would run before morning, and He loved them to the end. He knows you just as well, and He has not changed His mind about you.

The dust has told you that love is a vow held up by your own grip. You know what it is to say the big thing at night and fold by morning. You have the broken vows to show for it — the promise at the altar that wore thin, the friend you said you would stand by, the word you gave your children. And when the grip failed, the dust told you to give up on love and keep your guard up for good. Peter would have understood. He swore he would lay down his life for his Lord, and before the rooster crowed he had denied Him three times.

So look at the order of things. Peter offered to die for Jesus. Jesus died for Peter. At a place near the city, the Good Shepherd laid down His life for sheep who had scattered, and Greater love has no one than this. Then He rose, and the grave gave Him back, and Peter’s story was not over. The love that held at the table held at the cross and held past the tomb. That is the love the new commandment comes from, and it was poured out on you before it was ever asked of you.

Take that love back into the week. When the man at church grates on you, remember the basin. When your wife needs you to make the first move, remember the bread He handed to the man who would betray Him. When the night comes and the old door stands open, stay at the table. And when you fail, as Peter did, hear the word Jesus spoke to a boaster before the boast had even broken: you will follow afterwards. He kept that word to Peter. The One who loved His own to the end has not stopped loving you.
closingVerse: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
carry: Jesus loved the eleven to the end, knowing every one of them would fail Him that night; whom will you love this week by that same measure, before he has earned it?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men have buried someone. You stood at the edge of the hole in a borrowed jacket and watched the box go down, and somebody read a verse about a house with many rooms. The words went over you like wind over a cut field. Then you drove home, and the house was quieter, and the dust started talking.

It says there is no house at the end — only the ground you are standing on. Or if there is something past the grave, it is fog, a guess, a story for children. And if there is a way to God at all, you will have to find it yourself, pave it with your own effort, and hope you guessed right. So a man keeps his head down and his heart braced. He lives like a renter: nothing is his for long, and the notice could come any day.

That is a troubled heart, and it lies down in the very dirt it is afraid of. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The psalmist did not ask for a clearer view of the road. He asked for a word that gives life, and a word is what Jesus gives in this chapter — a word spoken by the One who is Himself the Word.
John 14 is the word Jesus spoke to troubled men on the night before the cross. He does not hand them a plan. He hands them Himself: I am the way, the truth, and the life.

sections.heading: The Same Night, the Same Table
pulls: The dust says there is no house at the end, only the ground. Jesus says there are many homes in His Father’s house — and that He would have told you if it were not so.
paras: The chapter number marks no pause. Moments ago Judas went out into the night. Jesus told the eleven He was leaving and they could not follow yet. He told Peter that before the rooster crowed he would deny Him three times. Then, to men who have just heard all of that, He says, Don’t let your heart be troubled. That is the ground these words are spoken on: a betrayal set in motion, a denial foretold, a Master about to leave.

Peter has already asked where He is going. Now Thomas and Philip press in with questions of their own, and each one is a question you have asked. How can we know the way? Then, show us the Father. Jesus answers every one of them with Himself, and He does it without a word of scorn for the asking. Keep that in view as you read. The answer to a troubled heart is not first a place. It is a Person, and the place is good because He is in it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: BELIEVE ALSO IN ME
paras: Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me. Jesus is not telling the eleven to cheer up. He is telling them where to put their weight. A troubled heart is a heart with nothing solid under it, and Jesus gives them something to stand on.

Listen to how He says it. Believe in God. Believe also in me. He sets faith in Himself right beside faith in God, with no step down between them. No prophet ever talked like that. No good teacher would dare. Only the Word who was with God and was God can put Himself on the same line as the Father and ask for the same trust. This is John’s whole aim in writing — that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

Do not miss who is speaking. A few verses back this same Jesus was troubled in spirit at the table. He was troubled at Lazarus’ grave. As the cross drew near He said, Now my soul is troubled. He does not tell you to settle your heart from a safe height. He has felt the shaking Himself, and He is about to carry the worst of it to the cross for you.

So the command comes with its ground. A man cannot calm his own heart by telling it to calm down. He can only rest it on Someone who will hold. Do not let your heart be troubled, because there is Someone to believe. Grace comes before duty here as everywhere. He gives you Himself first, and then tells you to rest your weight on what He gave.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A PLACE MADE READY
paras: In my Father’s house are many homes. Jesus is going home, and He speaks of it the way a son speaks of his father’s place: plenty of room. Then He adds a line every grieving man should underline: If it weren’t so, I would have told you. Jesus does not flatter. He told Peter about the rooster. He told the crowds hard things, and many of them walked away. If there were no room for you, He would have said so. A man who has buried his father needs that sentence more than he needs a description of the rooms.

I am going to prepare a place for you. How does He prepare it? By going. The road He takes to His Father runs through the betrayal, the trial, the cross, and a tomb that could not keep Him. Everything that stood between a sinner and the Father’s house, He takes out of the way on that road. Your room was not built by your good months. It was made ready by His blood.

I will come again, and will receive you to myself; that where I am, you may be there also. This is His one return at the end of the age. It is not a stopover on the way to something better. What He brings then is the home itself — God dwelling with His people in a new creation. Revelation puts it plainly: Behold, God’s dwelling is with people. And notice what makes it home. Not the size of the rooms. Where I am. The house is good because He is in it.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE WAY IS A MAN
pulls: Thomas asked for directions, and Jesus gave him a Person. He does not point down a road and wish you luck. He is the road, and it runs all the way to the Father’s house.
paras: You know where I go, and you know the way. Thomas will not let that pass. Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way? It is an honest question, and Jesus does not scold him for it. He answers it better than Thomas asked it.

I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me. Thomas wanted directions. Jesus gave him a Person. He does not point down a road and wish you luck. He is the road. He is the truth about God, told in flesh and blood. He speaks the truth, and He is the truth. He is the life that death could not hold. And He is the only one.

That line offends men, and it is meant plainly. There are not many roads up the mountain. There is one way to the Father, and His name is Jesus Christ. Your church attendance is not a way. Your decent life is not a way. Your father’s faith is not a way. But hear the warmth in it too. This narrow word comes from the One who said, He who comes to me I will in no way throw out. The one way is open to every man who comes. You do not have to find it. It came down looking for you.

If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on, you know him, and have seen him. The way does not only lead to the Father. In Jesus, the Father has already come out to meet you on the road.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: SHOW US THE FATHER
paras: Philip asks for one more thing. Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us. Jesus answers him by name: Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father. Every meal, every healing, every word at the well and the grave — all of it was the Father, shown in His Son. I am in the Father, and the Father in me.

Then comes a promise men have bent out of shape. He who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father. Greater, not as if a man could out-heal Jesus, but greater in reach. When Jesus goes to the Father, He sends the Counselor, and the word about Him goes out to the uttermost parts of the earth. Dead men raised to life through the preaching of Christ in every nation — that is the greater work, and it is still going on.

Whatever you will ask in my name, I will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. This is not a blank check with His signature at the bottom. To ask in His name is to ask as His — for what fits His name, His purposes, His glory. A man who asks like that will find that Jesus keeps His word: If you will ask anything in my name, I will do it. The promise is wide, and its aim is the Father’s glory in the Son. A son asks his father for what fits the family name, and he asks without fear, because he knows whose house he lives in.

stations.verse: Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me.
stations.question: Jesus said Don’t let your heart be troubled to men who had just heard of betrayal and denial, and told them to believe in Him; what trouble have I been trying to settle every way but by trusting Him?
stations.gloss: to stir up; to trouble, to unsettle
body: Tarassō means to stir up or disturb. It can be used of water: John uses it of the pool at Bethesda, where the sick man waited for the water to be stirred up. More often it is used of the heart — to unsettle it, to throw it into turmoil. It stands in seventeen verses of the New Testament.

Three times before this verse, John uses the word of Jesus Himself — at Lazarus’ tomb, as the hour of the cross came near, and at the table when He named the betrayer. The One who says Don’t let your heart be troubled has been troubled Himself. He knows the stirred-up heart from the inside.

The dust says a troubled heart proves you have no faith, so you hide it. Jesus does not shame the shaking. He gives it somewhere to land: Believe in God. Believe also in me. A stirred heart can settle on Him, because He carried the trouble that mattered most to the cross.
stations.live: Write John 14:1 on a card and keep it where your worry starts — the bill drawer, the nightstand, the visor of the truck. When the stirring comes, read it aloud: ‘I believe in God. I believe also in You.’

stations.verse: In my Father’s house are many homes. If it weren’t so, I would have told you. I am going to prepare a place for you.
stations.question: Jesus told the eleven, In my Father’s house are many homes. If it weren’t so, I would have told you; what grief in me needs to rest on His plain word that there is room?
stations.gloss: a dwelling; a place where one stays
body: Monē is formed from the verb that means to remain or abide. It names a staying, and then a place to stay — a dwelling, a home. It appears in only two verses of the New Testament, both in this chapter.

The first is here: In my Father’s house are many homes. The second comes a few verses later, when Jesus says that He and the Father will come to him, and make our home with him — with the man who loves Him and keeps His word. One is the home Christ is preparing for you. The other is the home God makes in you now. The staying begins before the moving.

The dust says you are always passing through — a renter, one notice from the road. Christ uses a word made from staying. He is not offering you a room for the night. He is offering you a home in His Father’s house, and no one will put you out of it.
stations.live: Name the loss that has made the grave feel final to you. Read John 14:2–3 over it this week, slowly, and say the words He staked His honesty on: ‘If it weren’t so, He would have told me.’

stations.verse: In my Father’s house are many homes. If it weren’t so, I would have told you. I am going to prepare a place for you.
stations.question: Jesus told men about to watch Him leave that His going was to prepare a place for you; where am I still trying to make myself ready for God instead of resting in the place Christ has made ready?
stations.gloss: to prepare; to make ready
body: Hetoimazō means to prepare, to make ready. It is used of getting a room ready for guests, as when the disciples made ready the Passover. It is used of God readying what He means to give: a kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, a city He has prepared for His people. Forty verses of the New Testament use it.

Jesus uses it twice in two verses: I am going to prepare a place for you. Then, If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again. The preparing is done by the going. His cross, His empty tomb, His return to the Father — that is the work of getting the room ready. Nothing is left for you to finish.

The dust says you must get yourself ready before God will have you — clean up, sober up, square up. But the one doing the preparing in this verse is Christ. You come in as a guest to a house He readied.
stations.live: When the old voice tells you to clean yourself up before you pray, pray anyway, and start with this: ‘Christ went to prepare a place for me. I come in on what He made ready.’

stations.verse: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.
stations.question: Thomas asked how they could know the way, and Jesus answered with Himself — I am the way, the truth, and the life; what have I been counting on to bring me to the Father that is not Christ?
stations.gloss: a way, road, or path
body: Hodos is the common word for a road or path — the road a traveler walks, and then the way a man lives. The New Testament has it in ninety-nine verses. In Acts the first believers were known simply as the Way. Hebrews speaks of a new and living way into God’s presence, opened through the flesh of Christ.

In John’s Gospel the word first appears on the lips of the Baptist: Make straight the way of the Lord. Here the Lord Himself says, I am the way. Thomas wanted a map. Jesus told him the road was standing in front of him, and it had a face.

The dust says every man must find his own way to God. Christ says the way is a Man, and He has already made the trip from the Father’s side down into the dust and back again. You do not build the road. You come by Him.
stations.live: End every prayer this week by naming the only way you came: ‘I come to You, Father, through Jesus Christ, and through no one and nothing else.’

stations.verse: Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.
stations.question: Philip asked, Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us, and Jesus answered that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father; what more have I been demanding from God than He has shown me in Jesus?
stations.gloss: to show; to make known
body: Deiknymi means to show — to put a thing before someone’s eyes, and so to make it known. You will find it in thirty-one verses. In John it gathers around the Son: the Father shows him all things that he himself does; Jesus says, I have shown you many good works from my Father; and on the evening of the resurrection he showed them his hands and his side.

So when Philip says Lord, show us the Father, he is asking for what has been in front of him the whole time. Philip wanted something more than Jesus. There is nothing more. He who has seen me has seen the Father.

The dust says God is hidden, and if He wanted you to know Him He would give you a sign you could not miss. He has. The Father has shown Himself in a Son with nail-scarred hands — hands He held out to frightened men so they would know Him. Look there.
stations.live: Read one scene from John’s Gospel each day this week — the well, the pool, the grave, the basin. After each, write one line: ‘Here the Father shows me that He is…’ and finish it from the text.

practices.title: CARRY THE FIRST THREE VERSES
practices.body: Commit John 14:1–3 to memory this week. Say it on the drive to work and again before you sleep. When the news is bad, or the fuel bill comes in high, or the old fear of death wakes you at three in the morning, do not argue with the fear. Say the words. Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me. Let His promise do the talking.

practices.title: GRIEVE WITH HIS WORD IN HAND
practices.body: Think of a believer you have buried. This week, read John 14:2–3 at the grave or with his picture in your hand. Thank God by name for the place Christ prepared for him and for the day He will come again. Grief is not unbelief, and you do not have to hide it. But let it be the grief of a man who has heard If it weren’t so, I would have told you.

practices.title: SAY THE ONE WAY PLAINLY
practices.body: Someone in your life thinks all roads lead to God, or that his decent life will get him there. Pray for him by name every day this week. When the door opens, tell him plainly and kindly what Jesus said: no one comes to the Father except through Him. Do not argue to win. Tell him the way is open, and that Christ has never thrown out a man who came.

practices.title: STOP ASKING FOR MORE THAN CHRIST
practices.body: When you catch yourself asking God for a sign, a feeling, or a door flung wide before you will trust Him, stop there. Philip asked for the same thing. Open John and look at Jesus instead — what He did, what He said, how He treated sinners. He who has seen me has seen the Father. Let that be your answer to the itch for something more.

practices.title: PRAY IN HIS NAME
practices.body: Write out your prayer list. Beside each request, ask one question: can I ask this so that the Father is glorified in the Son? Some requests will stand. Pray those boldly every day, resting on His word, I will do it. Some will need rewriting — the raise you want for your pride, the outcome you want for your comfort. Bring those too, but bring them as His, and let Him answer as He sees best.

title: The Way, the Truth, and the Life
subtitle: from dust to the Father’s house
keyVerse: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.

passage.text: “Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me.
In my Father’s house are many homes. If it weren’t so, I would have told you. I am going to prepare a place for you.
If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and will receive you to myself; that where I am, you may be there also.
You know where I go, and you know the way.”
Thomas said to him, “Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?”
Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.
If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on, you know him, and have seen him.”
Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.”
Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father. How do you say, ‘Show us the Father?’
Don’t you believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? The words that I tell you, I speak not from myself; but the Father who lives in me does his works.
Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me; or else believe me for the very works’ sake.
Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father.
Whatever you will ask in my name, I will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
If you will ask anything in my name, I will do it.

stationsIntro: Read each verse as if you had just heard about the traitor and the rooster yourself, because the eleven had. Answer plainly, then let the Greek word walk you back to the One who is the way home.
lifeIntro: Before He asked the eleven for anything, Jesus told them what He was about to do: go, prepare a place, come again, and receive them to Himself. He is the way, and He has already walked it. These practices are how a man lives once he knows the house is ready and the road has a name. None of it earns a room. The room is already made, and the door is open.
lifePulls: Jesus did not hand troubled men a map and wish them well. He gave them Himself, went ahead to make the room ready, and promised to come back for them. That is the ground under your feet this week.
prayer: Father, Your Son has gone to prepare a place for me in Your house. Thank You that He gave me Himself — the way, the truth, and the life. Thank You that in Him I have seen You, and I need no other sign. When my heart is troubled this week, turn it to believe in You and in Him. Forgive me for trusting my own road and my own record to bring me to You. Comfort me over the ones I have buried in Christ, and keep me sure of the room He has made ready. Teach me to ask in His name, for Your glory in Your Son and not for my comfort alone. Thank You that He will come again and receive me to Himself, so that where He is, I will be also. Send the word of Christ through Your church to men who do not yet know the way. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: On the night He was betrayed, Jesus told troubled men to believe in God and in Him. He was going to His Father’s house to prepare a place, and He will come again to receive His own. Thomas asked for directions and got a Person: the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Him, and no one who comes is thrown out. Leave your own road. Come to the Father by Him.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the house that is not made of dust. There are many homes in it. There is room in it. There is a place in it made ready by the One who went ahead of you, and there is a Son in it, at His Father’s side, who said He would come back for you. He has never once told you a comfortable lie, and He did not start with this one.

The dust has been telling you the grave is the end of the road, or that past it lies only fog. It has told you that if there is a way to God at all, you will have to find it and pave it yourself and hope you guessed right. You have stood at gravesides with that voice in your ear. You have lain awake under it. It has kept your heart braced and your hands closed for years. It has made you grip this world as if it were the only house you will ever have.

But hear the One who was troubled at the grave and troubled at the table and went on to the cross anyway. He did not stay dead. He went to His Father by way of the cross, the new tomb in the garden, and the morning it stood open, and every step of that road was the preparing of your room. I am the way, the truth, and the life. You do not have to find the road. The road came down into the dust to find you, and it leads all the way home.

Keep His words close this week. When the news is bad, Believe in God. Believe also in me. When you stand by a grave, If it weren’t so, I would have told you. When you catch yourself asking for more than Christ, remember Philip, and look again at the Son who shows you the Father. When men tell you there are many roads, remember there is one, and it is open to whoever comes. He said, I will come again, and will receive you to myself. He will. And where He is, you will be there also.
closingVerse: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.
carry: Jesus said, No one comes to the Father, except through me, and He has opened that way to you by His cross; what road of your own will you stop walking this week?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men can name the day somebody left. A father who packed a bag and did not come back for supper. A foreman who said he would send for you and took a job three counties over. A friend who moved away and quit calling after the first winter. You learned early to stand on your own two feet, and you were proud of it. Nobody was coming, so you came for yourself.

The dust takes that lesson and lays it over God. It tells you Jesus was real, but He was there and you are here. He walked out of the tomb, went up into heaven, and left you a book and a list of rules. So you keep the rules the way a man keeps his late father’s tools — oiled, hung on the wall, and used out of duty with nobody in the room. Obedience turns into iron weight. Prayer turns into talk aimed at a ceiling.

That is an orphan’s faith, and it grinds a man down to powder. The psalm does not pretend otherwise, and it does not reach for grit. It reaches for God’s voice: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The man flat on the ground does not need a better plan. He needs God to speak.

In John 14, God speaks. Jesus tells eleven shaken men that He is leaving — and that He is not leaving them alone. I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever. The Son goes to the Father. The Spirit comes from the Father. And the Spirit stays.

sections.heading: The Last Night, the Longest Talk
pulls: The dust says Christ left and you were left to manage. Jesus says He asked the Father, and the Father sent another Counselor — not for a season, not for the good weeks, but to be with you forever.
paras: This is still the night of the supper. The feet have been washed. Judas Iscariot has gone out into the dark. Peter has been told he will deny his Lord before the rooster crows. Jesus has said, Don’t let your heart be troubled, and promised a Father’s house with room in it. Thomas has asked his question, and Philip his. Before the night is over, another Judas — John is careful to say, not Iscariot — will ask one more.

What Jesus gives in answer to all of it is a Person. Not a method for coping with His absence, but the Holy Spirit Himself, sent by the Father in the Son’s name. Read 14:15–31 straight through before you go on. Count how many times Jesus says He will do something, and how many times He says the Father will. Then notice what He asks of you. It comes after the gifts, and it comes plain: love Him, keep His word, and do not be afraid.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: ANOTHER COUNSELOR
paras: Jesus opens with a sentence men have turned into a whip. If you love me, keep my commandments. Read in a hurry, it sounds like a test He sets to find out whether your love is real. But listen to what He says next, before He draws breath. I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor. The command and the gift come in the same breath. He does not hand you a load and walk off. He hands you the load and the One who will carry it in you.

Look hard at the word another. Jesus has been their Counselor for three years. He taught them, corrected them, fed them, washed their feet, and stood between them and the storm. Now He promises a second One like Himself. The Spirit is not a force or a mood. He is a Person, sent by the Father at the Son’s asking — one God, Father, Son and Spirit, all at work for eleven frightened men and for you.

Then notice where He will live. He lives with you, and will be in you. Earlier in this Gospel, John told you the Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn’t yet glorified (7:39). The cross, the empty grave and the Son’s return to the Father had to come first. They have come. If you belong to Christ, the Spirit has not merely called on you. He has moved in, and the world that cannot see Him cannot evict Him either.
That is why the command does not crush. Love for Christ does not come up out of your own dust. The Spirit works it in you, answering what Christ has already done for you.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: NOT LEFT AS ORPHANS
paras: I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you. Jesus picks the word every abandoned boy knows in his bones. An orphan has a name and nobody to give it to. He sleeps under somebody else’s roof and waits to be told to move along. Christ says that will not be you. He will come — alive out of the grave to stand among them again, and by His Spirit, who brings the risen Lord near.

Then comes the line to carry in your shirt pocket. Because I live, you will live also. Your life hangs on His, not His on yours. Within a day the world will stop seeing Him. They will nail Him to a cross and lay Him in a tomb. But His own will see Him alive, and their life is bound to His. He cannot die again, so neither can the life He gives them.

Judas — the other Judas — asks why Jesus will show Himself to them and not to the world. Jesus answers with a house. If a man loves me, he will keep my word. My Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our home with him. Earlier that night He spoke of rooms made ready in the Father’s house. Now He says the Father and the Son will come and live in the man who loves Him. Before you ever go to His house, He comes to yours.

The man who does not love Christ does not keep His words, because the words are the Father’s and he does not know the Father. The man who loves Him keeps them — not to buy a visit, but because Someone already lives there.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE TEACHER WHO REMINDS
pulls: The Spirit does not add to what Christ said. He reminds you of it. Fill a man with the words of Jesus, and the Spirit will have something to bring back to him in the dark.
paras: I have said these things to you while still living with you. Jesus knows how much of this night they will lose. Within hours they will be scattered, every man to his own place. Peter will stand by a fire in a courtyard and say he does not know Him. Three years of teaching, and by morning most of it will feel like smoke off a burn pile.

So He makes them a promise about their memory. But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you. Watch that promise keep itself. More than once John admits the disciples did not understand a thing when it happened, and then remembered it after Jesus was raised and glorified (2:22; 12:16). The Gospel in your hands is that remembering, written down. The Spirit taught the apostles, and the apostles wrote.

That matters on an ordinary Tuesday. The Spirit does not hand you a fresh word to set beside Scripture or above it. He opens the word He already gave. He takes what Christ said and presses it into you when you need it — the verse that comes back in the hospital hallway, the promise that rises when the old sin knocks at the back door, the line from John you did not know you had kept. You are not left to guess what God thinks. He has spoken, and the Spirit makes you hear it.
So the man who wants the Spirit’s help goes where the Spirit speaks. He fills himself with the words of Jesus, and he gives the Teacher something to bring back.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: PEACE LEFT BEHIND
paras: Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you. A dying man leaves things behind. A little land, a tool chest, a pickup, sometimes a debt. Jesus is hours from the cross, and what He leaves is His own peace — the same peace with which He will walk out to meet the soldiers. Not as the world gives, I give to you. The world gives peace by taking the trouble away. Christ gives it in the middle of the trouble, because the trouble cannot reach what He has given.

So He says it again. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful. This is no scolding. It is a Son speaking to frightened men with His arm already around them. The fear is real. The peace is more real, because it rests on Him and not on how the night goes.

Then a hard word: If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I said ‘I am going to my Father;’ for the Father is greater than I. The Son is not less God than the Father — John opened his Gospel by saying the Word was God. But the Son has come down. He has taken flesh, taken the servant’s place, and is on His way to a cross. Going to the Father means the humbling is nearly over and the glory is near. Love would be glad for Him.

The prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me. Satan has no claim on Jesus — no sin, no debt, no handle to grab. Christ goes to the cross that the world may know that I love the Father. Then He stands up from the table. Arise, let’s go from here. Your peace was bought on that walk.

stations.verse: I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever.
stations.question: On the night He said He was leaving, Jesus promised the Father would give another Counselor, that he may be with you forever; where am I living this week as if Christ went away and left me to manage alone?
stations.gloss: other, another; a second one alongside the first
body: Allos is a plain word: other, another. The New Testament uses it in 136 verses. Greek had a second word for other, one that leans toward a difference in kind. Allos simply counts a second one beside the first.

That is the word Jesus chooses. He has been their Counselor at close range — teaching, correcting, guarding, feeding. Now He promises another Counselor, a second beside Himself, not a lesser help sent to fill in. The Spirit will be to them what Jesus has been, and He will not leave at the end of three years. He will be with you forever.

The dust says you had Christ once — at the altar, at your baptism, in the good year — and now you are on your own. Allos says the Father sent a second Counselor so that you would never be on your own again. The help did not end when Jesus went to the Father. It moved in.
stations.live: When you catch yourself facing something alone this week, stop and say it out loud before you go on: ‘The Father gave me another Counselor. He is with me forever.’

stations.verse: The Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive; for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you, and will be in you.
stations.question: Jesus said the world can’t receive the Spirit because it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him, but told His own, he lives with you; where am I judging God’s nearness by what I can see instead of by Christ’s promise?
stations.gloss: to look at, behold; to see, perceive
body: Theōreō comes from the word for a spectator. It means to look at, to watch, and in ordinary speech simply to see or perceive. John reaches for it in twenty-two verses, more than any other book, and can even use it for experiencing a thing: the man who keeps Christ’s word will never see death (8:51).

Here the world doesn’t see him. It watches only for what it can measure — wind on its face, a man it can send a bill to. The Spirit gives it none of that, so it decides nothing is there. Two verses later the word turns: the world will see Jesus no more, but you will see me.

The dust wants proof you could weigh at the feed store. Jesus says you know the Spirit because he lives with you. The faith that clings to Christ, the hunger for His word, the grief when you sin — you did not grow those. That is the unseen Spirit at work.
stations.live: Write down three things in you that were not there before Christ found you — a love, a sorrow, a hunger. Do not take credit for any of them. Thank the Father for the Spirit who put them there.

stations.verse: But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.
stations.question: Jesus promised the Spirit would remind you of all that I said to you, and that remembering now stands written in the Gospels; what am I asking God to tell me that He has already said in His Word?
stations.gloss: to teach; to instruct a person in a thing
body: Didaskō is the common New Testament word for teaching, found in 90 verses. In 14:26 it takes two objects at once: the Spirit will teach you, and He will teach all things. A person is taught, and something is handed over.

All things here does not mean every fact under heaven. It means all that Christ said, brought back and made plain. The Spirit taught the apostles, and their teaching stands written. That is why John could later tell a church that already had the apostles’ word that the anointing teaches you concerning all things (1 John 2:27).
The dust says God has gone quiet and you must work out His will by guesswork. But the Teacher has not left the room. He teaches through the very words He once taught.
stations.live: Read John 14 aloud once this week, start to finish. Before you begin, ask plainly: ‘Spirit of truth, teach me what Christ said, and bring it back to me when I need it.’

stations.verse: Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.
stations.question: Hours before His arrest, Jesus handed His men His own peace and said, Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful; what fear have I been treating as stronger than the peace He left me?
stations.gloss: to be timid, fearful; to play the coward
body: Deiliaō means to be timid, fearful, even cowardly. This verse is the only place in the New Testament where it appears. Jesus sets it beside the word for a troubled heart that opened the chapter, so that the night begins and ends with the same comfort: Don’t let your heart be troubled.

This is the fear that makes a man shrink. He goes quiet when he ought to speak. He sits in the parking lot when he ought to walk in. He lets the hard phone call slide into a third week. Jesus names that fear on the night His men will scatter, and He names it gently, having just given them His peace.

The dust says courage is something you have to dig up in yourself. Christ says peace is something He leaves you. Stop digging for nerve. Stand on what He gave: My peace I give to you. A man with the peace of Christ in him does not need to play the coward.
stations.live: Name the conversation or task you have shrunk from out of fear. Before you take it up this week, say: ‘He left me His peace. I do not have to find my own.’ Then go and do it.

stations.verse: You heard how I told you, ‘I go away, and I come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I said ‘I am going to my Father;’ for the Father is greater than I.
stations.question: Jesus told grieving men that if they loved Him they would have rejoiced that He was going to the Father; what would change in me this week if I counted His going as my gain rather than my loss?
stations.gloss: great; in its comparative form, greater
body: Megas means great — great in size, in degree, or in rank. It stands in 228 verses of the New Testament. Here it comes in its comparative form, greater. John uses that same form for the Father who is greater than all (10:29) and for the love that lays down its life (15:13).

So when Jesus says the Father is greater than I, He is speaking of His place that night, not of what He is. The Word who was God has come down to the servant’s place. He is about to go back up, by way of the cross, to the Father who sent Him. That is why He tells them love would rejoice. The Son is going home.

The dust wants you to measure everything by what it costs you. The eleven were about to lose Jesus from their table. But His going was their gain, and yours: He went to the Father, and the Spirit came. Greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world.
stations.live: When grief over a loss crowds your thinking this week, add one line to your prayer and mean it: ‘Christ has gone to the Father, and He reigns there for me.’

practices.title: KEEP HIS WORD IN REACH
practices.body: Jesus promised the Spirit would remind you of all that I said to you. He brings back what has been put in. Read one chapter of John each morning this week — 14 through 16, and then around again — before the phone comes on. Write one verse on a card and keep it in your shirt pocket. When the Spirit brings it back on Wednesday afternoon in the middle of a bad hour, you will know where it came from.

practices.title: QUIT LIVING LIKE AN ORPHAN
practices.body: Orphans hoard. They keep their own counsel and plan for nobody coming. Find the place where you have been living that way — the money you keep out of sight, the decision you will not talk over with your wife, the worry you carry by yourself at two in the morning. Bring it into the open this week, first to God and then to her. You have a Father who loves you and a Counselor who lives with you.

practices.title: LOVE HIM, THEN KEEP HIS WORD
practices.body: Before you open the day’s list, say in one sentence what Christ has done for you. Then take the one command of His you have been dodging — the apology you owe, the honest number on the form, the kind word your son has gone without — and keep it. You are not buying His love with it. The One who gave Himself for you has made His home with you, and a man keeps the word of the One who lives under his roof.

practices.title: TAKE THE PEACE HE LEFT
practices.body: Fear will come this week with a face on it — a doctor’s call, a rumor of layoffs, a teenager out past midnight. When it comes, do not go hunting for your own calm. Say His words back to Him: Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you. Then do the next plain thing in front of you, as a man who has been left something no one can take away.

practices.title: STAND UP AND GO
practices.body: Arise, let’s go from here. Jesus stood up from the table and walked toward the cross, for love of the Father and for you. This week, when your time in the Word ends, do not just close the book and reach for your coffee. Get up and do one thing the passage put in front of you before the day swallows it. The Counselor does not stay in the chair. He goes with you out the door.

title: Another Counselor
subtitle: from dust to the Spirit who stays
keyVerse: I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever.

passage.text: If you love me, keep my commandments.
I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever:
the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive; for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you, and will be in you.
I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you.
Yet a little while, and the world will see me no more; but you will see me. Because I live, you will live also.
In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.
One who has my commandments and keeps them, that person is one who loves me. One who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and will reveal myself to him.”
Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, “Lord, what has happened that you are about to reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?”
Jesus answered him, “If a man loves me, he will keep my word. My Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our home with him.
He who doesn’t love me doesn’t keep my words. The word which you hear isn’t mine, but the Father’s who sent me.
I have said these things to you while still living with you.
But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.
Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.
You heard how I told you, ‘I go away, and I come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I said ‘I am going to my Father;’ for the Father is greater than I.
Now I have told you before it happens so that when it happens, you may believe.
I will no more speak much with you, for the prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me.
But that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father commanded me, even so I do. Arise, let’s go from here.

stationsIntro: Read each verse aloud and slowly, the way a man reads the last words his father left him. Answer the question in plain words, then let the Greek turn you back to the Spirit who was sent to stay.
lifeIntro: The Father has given another Counselor. The Son has promised not to leave you an orphan, and the Father and the Son have come to make their home with the man who loves Christ. Five plain responses follow — not the rent on that home, but the way a man lives in it.
lifePulls: You do not obey to bring the Spirit near. He was sent, He lives with you, and He will be in you. Obedience is what a man does in a house where God has already come to stay.
prayer: Father, You heard Your Son’s prayer and gave us another Counselor. Thank You that the Spirit of truth lives with us and is in us, and that the world cannot take Him away. Thank You that Jesus did not leave us orphans, and that because He lives, we will live also. Make Your home with me, and teach me to keep the word of Your Son because I love Him. Bring back to my mind what Christ has said, on the day I need it most. Forgive me for the fear that shrinks me and the silence that hides me. Give me the peace Jesus left, the peace the world did not give and cannot take. Keep me glad that my Lord has gone to You and reigns there. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You heard Your Son’s prayer and gave us another Counselor.
Thank You that the Spirit of truth lives with us and is in us, and that the world
cannot take Him away.
Thank You that Jesus did not leave us orphans, and that because He lives, we will
live also.
Make Your home with me, and teach me to keep the word of Your Son because I
love Him.
Bring back to my mind what Christ has said, on the day I need it most.
Forgive me for the fear that shrinks me and the silence that hides me.
Give me the peace Jesus left, the peace the world did not give and cannot take.
Keep me glad that my Lord has gone to You and reigns there.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Jesus did not leave His men to manage on their own. He asked the Father, and the Father sent another Counselor, the Holy Spirit, to be with them forever and to live in them. The Spirit teaches what Christ said and brings it back to mind. Christ left His own peace, went to the Father, and met the prince of this world with nothing in Him to grab. You are not an orphan. Stop living like one.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the Son who prayed for you before you knew how to pray. Lift them to the Father who heard Him and gave. Lift them to the Spirit of truth, sent in the Son’s name, who did not come for a visit and will not pack up when the year goes bad. He lives with you. He is in you. He is with you forever.

The dust has told you that Christ was real but far off, that He left you a rulebook and an empty chair. Some days you have kept His commands the way a man keeps his dead father’s tools — out of duty, alone, with no one watching. But hear Him on the last night. I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you. He did not walk out of your life. He went to the Father so that the Counselor could walk in.

Look at Him standing up from that table. The prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me. He went out into the night, across the brook, into the hands of men, carrying no sin of His own and all of yours. He laid down His life, and He took it up again. Because I live, you will live also. You do not have to hold that hope up by your own strength. Your life is bound to His, and His will never end. So carry this into Tuesday. When the house is quiet and the fear is loud, you are not alone in the room. The Father and the Son have made their home with you. The Spirit will bring back what Christ said — this very word, if you keep it near, on the morning you need it most. And the peace Jesus left is still yours, His own peace, the kind the world did not give and cannot repossess. Stand up from the table, then, and go. The Son asked, the Father gave, and the Counselor He sent is with you forever.
closingVerse: I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever.
carry: If the Father has given you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever, what will you stop carrying alone this week as though no one had come?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man knows the pressure to produce. The bid has to land. The field has to yield. The paycheck has to stretch to the last week of the month. You were raised to believe a man is what he brings in, and in the year you bring in nothing, you feel like nothing.

The dust carries that straight into your life with God. It tells you fruit is a quota. Be more patient, pray longer, give more, quit the habit, lead your house — and get it done by Friday on your own steam. So you set your jaw and crank it out. Some weeks it looks fine from the road. Up close the rows are dry, and you are tired in a way a night’s sleep does not touch.

The dust talks loud, but it does not get the last word. God does, and the psalm goes straight to Him: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) Not revive me by a better effort. Revive me by what You say.

Jesus answers with a picture any man who has ever grown a row of beans or a backyard grape arbor can follow. I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. A branch does not strain. It holds on, and the life comes up through it from a root it did not plant.

sections.heading: Spoken on the Way to the Garden
pulls: The dust says fruit is a quota you fill on your own steam. Christ says He is the vine and you are a branch. Branches do not manufacture grapes. They hold on, and the life of the vine does the rest.
paras: Jesus has just said, Arise, let’s go from here. John does not tell you where the next words are spoken, only that they come before Jesus crosses the brook Kidron into the garden (18:1). It is still the last night. Judas has gone. The cross is hours away. And Jesus tells eleven men how they will live when He is no longer at the table — joined to Him the way a branch is joined to its vine.

The picture is old. The psalmist said to God, You brought a vine out of Egypt (Psalm 80:8), and Isaiah sang of a vineyard planted with care that yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:2). Jesus takes up that picture and says, I am the true vine. What Israel never was, He is, and every man joined to Him is joined to the true people of God. Read 15:1–17 through twice. Count how often He says remain, and how often He says love. Then notice which one comes first.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE VINE AND THE FARMER
paras: I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer. Before Jesus says one word about you, He tells you who He is and who His Father is. The life is His. The tending is the Father’s. You are neither the root nor the one holding the shears. That should lift a weight off your back before the second verse, and it should change how you read every verse after it.

Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit. Two kinds of branches, two kinds of cutting. One is cut off because nothing comes through it. The other is cut back because something does. The Father’s knife on a living branch is care, not punishment. He takes off the growth that drinks the sap and bears nothing — the pride, the hobby that turned into an idol, the second drink, the comfort you would not give up — so that more of His Son’s life can show in you.

Then Jesus says something to steady you. You are already pruned clean because of the word which I have spoken to you. Already. The eleven are clean, not because they have finished growing, but because Christ has spoken His word over them. The cleansing came first. The pruning that follows comes to a branch that is already His.

So when the cut comes this year — the plan that died, the money that went, the friendship that ended — do not read it as the Father walking off the place. A farmer does not prune what he means to burn. He prunes what he means to keep, and he keeps it for the harvest.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: REMAIN IN ME
paras: Remain in me, and I in you. Here is the one command at the center of the picture, and it comes wrapped in a promise. Christ does not say, Produce for Me. He says, Stay where I have put you. And He binds Himself to it: and I in you. You remain in Him, and He remains in you. The holding goes both ways, and His grip is the stronger one.

As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me. A cut branch on the ground can look green for a day. Leave it in the sun and see. Then Jesus shuts every back gate: apart from me you can do nothing. Not a little. Nothing. No real patience, no real love for your wife, no real hatred of sin grows out of your own wood.

How does a man remain? Jesus says it in the next breath: His words remaining in you (15:7), and you remaining in His love (15:9). That means the plain means He gave — His word, prayer and the Lord’s Supper. You do not use them to earn the vine’s life. You use them to stay where that life flows.

Then the warning. If a man doesn’t remain in me, he is thrown out as a branch and is withered, gathered and burned. This is not a true branch losing its hold.
